ideas.title: Ready-to-Build: the constraint-clearing layer for line crews
ideas.one_liner: Sell line contractors and utility construction departments a live 'ready backlog' in which every job is gated on the six things that actually idle a crew, and charge per crew-month.
ideas.customer: Line contractors with 40-500 crews on unit-price or time-and-equipment MSAs, plus utility construction and distribution operations departments that run in-house crews (about half of all line workers per BLS). First 10: independent contractors with 40-150 crews serving two or three IOUs (not Quanta or MasTec, who build in-house).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Contractor VP Operations or COO from operating budget (on unit-price work every recovered crew-hour is margin). For utilities: Director of Construction or Distribution Operations from the contractor-oversight / construction-management line. MYR's 10-K says MSA work is billed unit-price, time-and-materials or time-and-equipment; I could not confirm what share of billed hours is standby (unverified).
ideas.problem: A crew (3-6 people plus 2-3 specialty trucks, roughly $0.6-1.0M a year, my estimate) earns only when six gates are open the same day: approved stake sheet, staged materials, outage/clearance window, live 811 locates, access/permits, traffic control. Six owners in four systems hold them, and the foreman keeps the status in his head and a group text. Bain found a utility's crew wrench time averaged about 40%. Transformers average 128 weeks of lead time (WoodMac), and over half the utility workforce has under 10 years' experience.
ideas.solution: Read jobs from the utility work-management system or contractor ERP; track the six gates with owners and due dates and chase owners by text/voice; publish a daily ready list ranked by crew qualification, travel and outage window; re-plan same-day when a gate fails by swapping in a ready job; keep an audit trail of standby caused by utility-side vs contractor-side gates (settles disputes, feeds prudence reviews). Scalable assets: per-utility gate rules and a cross-utility benchmark of outage-window cancellations and gate-failure rates.
ideas.why_now: Record backlogs (Quanta $53.4B, Dycom $9.5B, MasTec Power Delivery about $4.8B guide) and capex up about 29% (S&P, 2026) make each idle crew-day the most expensive ever; 128-week transformers and a thinner-experience workforce remove the slack tribal knowledge used to cover; Quanta absorbing 7,400 employees via four acquisitions leaves independents looking for an edge.
ideas.wedge: A 'Standby Autopsy': 60 days of timecards and field tickets from 10 crews sorted by cause, sold as a $15k diagnostic that converts to $2,500 per crew-month. Start with outage-window and materials-staging gates on distribution rebuild programs.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption: about 33k US crews (BLS 131.9k line installers/repairers, 2025, divided by about 4; half are utility in-house). At $2,500 per crew-month ($30k a year, about 4% of a crew's annual billings, about a third of the value of a 10% productivity gain), 3,300 crews = $99M, i.e. about 10% of all crews, reached through roughly 50 organizations with 60+ crews each. Gross margin 65-70% (assumption).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Locusview/Itron (as-built capture, close-out, invoicing; about 4,000 crews a day, 30+ utilities), utility work-management systems (Maximo, SAP, Oracle, IFS; readiness features not verified), Assignar and Planera (general-construction scheduling), Utilen (utility-supplier materials coordination, seed Dec 2025), Quanta's in-house tools, spreadsheets and group texts. I found no product built around the six gates for T&D crews.
ideas.why_they_lose: The utility's system cannot see the contractor's yard or crew qualifications; the contractor's system cannot see the utility's outage calendar; Locusview records work after it happens; general-construction schedulers do not know clearances or 811 tickets; the biggest contractors will never sell their tools to rivals. Main risk: Itron bundles readiness into Locusview.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (it becomes the daily dispatch routine) plus a cornered resource (cross-utility outage-window and gate-failure data).
ideas.earned_secret: Standby is billed, so nobody inside the utility sees it as waste until an audit. The costliest idle hour is the 5:30 a.m. call when system operations cancels the outage window, because the three people who knew it was fragile were never told. (Insider claim; the share of hours is unverified and is what the first pilots measure.)
ideas.first_90_days: Sign three superintendents as design partners; run the Standby Autopsy by hand for 10 crews; build read-only imports from Maximo/SAP exports and 811 ticket status; stand up a human 'readiness desk' that chases gate owners by phone; close two paid pilots at $2,500 per crew-month.

ideas.title: Zero-Redline: outcome-priced distribution work packages
ideas.one_liner: A vendor-neutral design pod that delivers construction-ready distribution work packages, priced per package accepted with zero redlines, using the incumbents' tools plus each utility's standards compiled into checks.
ideas.customer: Co-ops and munis with design backlogs, mid-size IOU customer-driven teams, and line contractors bidding design-build MSAs. First 10: 4 co-ops/munis, 3 design-build contractors, 3 mid-size IOU teams.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Utility Director of Distribution Engineering or VP Engineering from the capitalized design line (design is 8-15% of construction cost in the benchmarks I found, all water/wastewater); for contractors, the VP Preconstruction.
ideas.problem: The software exists (SBS, Itron, GSI, Bentley) but the designers do not. Vendors estimate 10-15% of projects need field correction or redesign at 4-8 hours each (vendor claim, unverified). Hourly engineering firms lose revenue if hours fall; contractors paid per unit lose scope if designs get leaner; so nobody is paid by the accepted package.
ideas.solution: Packages are field-verified (imagery, LiDAR, street-level plus a foreman photo check), standards-checked (rules compiled from the utility's construction standards), complete with BOM, compatible units, permit/easement flags, and PE-stamped where needed. Priced per package accepted, free rework on any redline. Pods (US lead plus nearshore) run licensed vendor tools. Over time the standards library and a 'why rejected' corpus become the checker; first-pass acceptance is the product metric.
ideas.why_now: Capex up about 29% against flat engineering headcount (vendor-sponsored claim); the design-software vendors have all been bought (SBS by Enverus, GSI by private equity, Locusview by Itron), so no neutral party sells outcomes.
ideas.wedge: One high-volume package type (single-phase overhead and underground service extensions) in two utilities' standards, sold first to design-build contractors who feel redlines in margin; measure first-pass acceptance on the first 500 packages.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption: T&D capex $100-120B x 9-12% design = $9-14B; about half outsourced = $4.5-7B. At $900-1,000 per package (construction value about $15k x 8-10%), 100-110k packages = $100M, i.e. 1.5-2.2% of outsourced design dollars, or about 5% of an assumed 2M design work orders a year (not sourced).
ideas.who_does_it_today: SBS AUD (Enverus is acquiring SBS), Itron Distribution Staker, GSI Distribution Design Studio (sold to a PE portfolio company Jan 2026), Bentley, Hexagon; hourly firms Burns & McDonnell, Sargent & Lundy, Black & Veatch, POWER Engineers, Ulteig, Kimley-Horn; offshore design BPOs (unverified); AI-native entrants Unlimited Industries ($12M seed, a16z), Tiros, AZX, Piq Energy, Gridsight.
ideas.why_they_lose: Software vendors sell seats and cannot carry rework risk; hourly firms lose revenue when hours fall; contractors lose units when designs shrink; AI-native startups chase hyperscaler/industrial EPC where tickets are larger. Risk: Enverus adds services to the SBS base.
ideas.moat: Process power (a rejection-learning loop that raises acceptance rate) with secondary switching costs once a utility's standards live in the checker.
ideas.earned_secret: The designer's real job is predicting what the crew will find in the field. Redlines cluster in three causes: stale GIS, an unrecorded customer change, a standard nobody told the contractor about. Fix those and you can price by outcome. (Insider claim, to be measured on the first 500 packages.)
ideas.first_90_days: Compile one package type for two utilities' standards; recruit 2 design-build contractors; deliver 100 packages at cost with a rework guarantee and log every redline by cause; set price from the measured acceptance rate.

ideas.title: Spec Passport: shared product qualification, paid by the suppliers
ideas.one_liner: Test a distribution product once and let many utilities accept it: free to utility standards engineers, paid for by the manufacturers who want onto approved-materials lists.
ideas.customer: Free side: standards and materials engineers at utilities. Paid side: manufacturers and importers of transformers, cutouts, arresters, connectors, insulators, poles, crossarms and conductor. First 10: 3 new US transformer plants, 4 importers, 3 hardware makers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Manufacturer VP of utility sales or director of product qualification, from the budget that already pays for samples, lab tests, trial installs, travel and consultants.
ideas.problem: Every utility keeps its own approved-materials list; trials run a year or longer (EWEB) and sit on waiting lists (Queen Creek). I found no utility that accepts another's product test data. With 128-week transformer lead times, utilities want alternates but cannot qualify them quickly, and a new supplier cannot afford 50 separate qualifications. The Nordics share supplier pre-qualification (SELLIHCA) and the UK has UVDB, but product-level reciprocity is missing.
ideas.solution: (1) Accredited-lab test protocols per category covering IEEE/ANSI/NEMA plus the top 25 utilities' extras; (2) a free Utility Console: side-by-side comparison against the utility's own spec, pooled field-trial results, alerts when a product fails elsewhere; (3) a Passport credential utilities opt to accept in place of repeat lab tests; (4) manufacturers pay for protocols and the Passport (fees buy testing and listing, never ranking); (5) later a sourcing desk routing urgent RFQs to passported alternates.
ideas.why_now: Transformer and hardware shortages (128-week transformers), steel/aluminum/copper tariffs, and new US capacity entrants who need many utilities to say yes at once; utility standards staff are thinner than ever.
ideas.wedge: Distribution transformers and cutouts, where alternates are most needed and test methods are standard. Anchor with 5 co-ops, one G&T and 2 IOUs that agree to read the data, plus 10 paying manufacturers on a $25k pilot.
ideas.path_to_100m: All inputs are assumptions or unverified. (a) Qualification fees: assume about 1,500 manufacturers/importers sell to US utilities, each spending about $400k a year on qualification = $600M pool; capturing 10% = $60M. (b) Sourcing desk: distribution materials about $24B (40% of about $60B distribution capex); routing 10% at 1.5% = $36M. (c) Utility data subscriptions: 100 x $100k = $10M. Total about $106M, needing 10% of an unverified spend pool and 10% of materials. Least certain size of the eight.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Every utility's own AML and trial process; UL Solutions (utility cable specs), Tecnalia (EU), SELLIHCA and UVDB (supplier-level only), Avetta/ISN/Veriforce (contractor safety, not products), Utilen (project/materials coordination), distributors with supplier programs (Wesco, Graybar, Border States). Possible free substitutes: EPRI/EEI/NRECA standardization work (not checked).
ideas.why_they_lose: Utilities cannot afford to publish failures or test for others; distributors and OEMs are not neutral; prequalification schemes certify companies, not products; nobody owns the cross-utility field-performance record.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more utilities accepting draws more manufacturers, and the reverse) plus a cornered resource (the pooled field-performance dataset).
ideas.earned_secret: An approved-materials list is mostly institutional memory, such as why a product failed at one co-op in 2011. Utilities do not share it because nobody is paid to write it down in a form another utility can use. The first party paid to do that, by the vendors who want in, becomes the record.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 standards engineers on what evidence would replace a repeat test; compile 8 utilities' transformer and cutout requirements; contract an ISO 17025 lab; sign 5 manufacturers to a paid pilot; launch the free console for 5 co-ops.

ideas.title: Capacity Upgrade Desk: limiting-element-first reconductoring, funded by the load
ideas.one_liner: Find the single span or terminal that actually limits each congested line, fix it, and reconductor only where it pays, with the data-center or industrial customer funding the work in exchange for deliverable capacity.
ideas.customer: Transmission owners with congested 69-230 kV corridors serving load pockets, and the developers who need deliverability. First 10: 5 utilities in constrained pockets (PJM, ERCOT, MISO, Southeast) and 5 funding developers.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Funding developer's VP Energy or Infrastructure, from interconnection capex (contribution in aid of construction or capacity-contribution agreement); the utility's VP Transmission Planning signs the scope and the PUC approves cost recovery.
ideas.problem: About 700,000 miles of lines, only about 1% reconductored or rebuilt a year. New lines take 10-15 years against 1-2 for reconductoring (vendor-sourced); advanced conductor costs 1.5-5x conventional (DOE). FERC Order 1920 requires consideration of advanced conductors and dynamic ratings and CA SB 1006 studies were due 2026-01-01, but studies rarely reach construction. Utilities earn a return on capex either way, and on many lines the limit is a terminal, clearance crossing or structure rather than the conductor (insider, unverified).
ideas.solution: LiDAR/imagery line survey with ratings reconciliation; limiting-element model across sag, clearance, structure and terminal equipment; ranking by MW gained per dollar and per month; design and bid packages that fix the limiting element and reconductor only where needed, with conductor specified from several makers; outage plans using Ready-to-Build; a template in which the developer funds the upgrade and receives capacity rights while the utility owns the asset and recovers cost through a rider; infrastructure funds pre-underwrite the contractual cash flows.
ideas.why_now: 1,066 GW of requested data-center load with only 12% firm (WoodMac, Aug 2026); FERC's 2026-06-18 show-cause orders ask RTOs to explain not using alternative transmission technologies; Google solicited advanced-conductor projects (Jun 2025); NJ S674 and the REWIRE Act of 2026 are pending.
ideas.wedge: A $150-400k limiting-element audit per corridor sold to a developer and a utility together; first 10 customers are 5 audits plus 5 follow-on design packages.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption: 7,000 miles a year (1% of 700,000) x 25% capacity-driven and addressable = 1,750 miles. Fees of about 12% on a roughly $1M-per-mile project (audit, engineering, program management) need about $830M of project value = about 830 miles = 12% of all miles. If it books turnkey EPC revenue instead, $100M is about 100 miles at $1M per mile (net margin about 10-12%).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Quanta (and Quanta Technology), MYR, Pike, Burns & McDonnell, Sargent & Lundy, POWER Engineers; conductor makers CTC Global, TS Conductor, Southwire, Prysmian; dynamic-rating vendors LineVision, Heimdall Power, Ampacimon; Google as a buyer, not a provider.
ideas.why_they_lose: EPC firms are paid by the mile of construction, so recommending a $2M terminal fix over a $40M reconductor cuts their scope; conductor makers sell wire; rating vendors sell sensors; utilities earn a return on the larger capex.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (neutral advice against EPC economics), then process power and a per-utility limiting-element library.
ideas.earned_secret: On most lines I worked, the conductor was not what limited the rating; one old terminal or one clearance crossing did. The cheapest megawatt on the system is at the weakest span.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit two transmission planners and a line engineer; offer one free limiting-element audit to a utility in a hyperscaler load pocket using existing NERC facility-rating data and a LiDAR subcontractor; draft the developer-funded capacity template with a utility lawyer and an infrastructure-fund contact.

ideas.title: Accredited Delivery Partner: customer-funded connections at the customer's speed
ideas.one_liner: Be the utility-accredited third party that designs, permits and builds customer-funded connections to the utility's standard, so customers who would pay to go faster can; a regulated utility structurally cannot sell that.
ideas.customer: Developers and owners with customer-funded extensions and upgrades: commercial and industrial campuses, 1-75 MW data-center and EV depots, subdivisions, municipal projects. First 10: 10 projects of 1-20 MW in California (applicant design under Rules 15/16) and Ohio (third-party installation to utility specs).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The customer's VP Development or construction director, from the utility-service / interconnection line of the project budget (the contribution in aid of construction they already pay).
ideas.problem: Utilities run first-in-first-out queues under non-discriminatory tariffs, cannot sell a priority lane or fixed date, and earn little on customer-contributed assets. PG&E's applicant-design guide says at least 5% of projects may take up to 357 days; the CPUC's 2024 energization targets (D.24-09-020) mostly report. SDG&E's 2026 guide lists 'customer dependencies' (approvals, payments, easement signatures, permits) that nobody manages. A delayed campus loses revenue every month.
ideas.solution: Accreditation per utility (the Ohio rule and NH statute contemplate approved contractors). A fixed-fee, fixed-date package: pre-application scoping, utility form filing, design to the utility's standard (Zero-Redline library), easement and permit management, long-lead procurement, construction by accredited crews, utility inspection and energization checklist. The partner books full contract value, subcontracts crews and keeps an assumed 12-18% margin. Per-utility cycle-time data becomes the reference regulators can cite. UK precedent: independent connection providers; Ofgem's Feb 2026 call for input proposes more self-build of high-voltage connection assets.
ideas.why_now: CPUC D.24-09-020 (2024) and D.26-02-025 (2026 flexible service connection offering); data-center and industrial load; Ofgem's 2026 reform direction. Legal premise checked: supported by CA Rules 15/16 and PG&E's applicant-design process, Ohio OAC 4901:1-9-07 and NH RSA 370:12; not found in Florida. State-by-state patchwork, so $100M needs three to five states or utility-run accreditation programs.
ideas.wedge: California customer-funded 1-10 MW projects with a signed will-serve letter, sold as 'energized by date X or we pay'.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption (no national figure found): distribution capex about $60B x 25-30% customer-driven = $15-18B; customer-funded and contestable where third parties are allowed today about 15-20% of that = $2.5-3.5B. Gross revenue of $100M is 3-4% of that pool; the net margin would be only $12-18M, so it works only if more states open or loads get larger.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Customers' civil engineers plus local line contractors, PG&E's applicant-design program, and in the UK the independent connection providers (they held about 8% of contestable electric connections in a 2008 dispute, and Ofgem found effective competition in 42 of 126 segments in 2010-15). Quanta and MasTec do not chase small customer-funded jobs. No national accredited-partner brand found (unverified).
ideas.why_they_lose: Utilities are barred from selling speed; engineers and contractors sell parts; the customer coordinating five parties is the bottleneck.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (accreditation by utilities) plus counter-positioning against the utility's own constraint.
ideas.earned_secret: Most delay is not engineering. It is the customer dependencies, such as easement signatures, permits, inspections and panel readiness, that nobody manages because the utility says it is the customer's job and the customer does not know how.
ideas.first_90_days: Get onto PG&E/SCE/SDG&E and one Ohio utility's approved-contractor or applicant-design lists; sign three customers to a fixed-date package; record the days spent at each step and each dependency.

ideas.title: Pooled Crews: a contract vehicle with reserved crews for co-ops and munis
ideas.one_liner: Pool about 2,800 small utilities' line construction, engineering and materials demand into a pre-competed multi-year vehicle with reserved crew-months, so small utilities stop being last in line behind Quanta's backlog.
ideas.customer: About 1,998 public power utilities (APPA 2026) and 864-905 distribution co-ops (NRECA). First 10: ten co-ops in one G&T system, signed through the G&T or statewide association.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Co-op GM and board, from the capital construction budget (RUS/CFC-financed work plans). The vehicle's fee is embedded in contractor pricing (as in other cooperative purchasing) plus an engineering subscription.
ideas.problem: Co-ops own 42% of line miles at 8 consumers per mile vs 32 elsewhere, with thin staff, a young workforce, 128-week transformers and last place in allocation. Big contractors optimize for large multi-year programs; a 15-pole job does not justify mobilization. Hourly engineers have minimums. A co-op cannot reserve crews alone because paying standby invites board and lender scrutiny. Sourcewell's electrical IDIQ awards include T&D services but are generalist and do not reserve capacity.
ideas.solution: Competitively bid multi-state MSAs with 3-5 qualified contractors including mid-size independents, unit-price rate cards, and crew-months reserved against aggregated member demand; a shared engineering pool (standard RUS units, staking, work plans, loan packages); pooled materials buying and a shared transformer spares pool; common inspection, safety and storm mutual-aid terms. Fee 2-3% of routed construction plus a $50-150k engineering subscription.
ideas.why_now: Contractor backlogs (Quanta $53.4B, Dycom $9.5B), capex up about 29%, data-center and industrial load reaching co-ops, and lead times that punish small buyers.
ideas.wedge: One G&T system's 10 co-ops: 36-month pipeline, 3 contractors, 20 reserved crew-months.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption (no sourced co-op/muni capex total): about $20B a year of capital spend, of which about $12B is construction, engineering and materials that could route through the vehicle. At 2.5%, $100M needs $4B routed (33% of $12B). Adding 300 members x $100k = $30M of engineering subscriptions lowers it to $2.8B routed, i.e. 14-20% of the pool. Heroic share; flagged.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Sourcewell/OMNIA/TIPS (generalist vehicles), NRECA, CFC and statewide associations (education, lobbying, finance), APPA mutual aid, engineering firms with co-op practices (not verified), and each utility's own RFP.
ideas.why_they_lose: Associations are non-profits that cannot underwrite crew capacity or take performance risk; general vehicles do not reserve crews; contractors cannot reserve for unknown demand.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in purchasing and a cornered resource (reserved crew capacity), with counter-positioning against the big contractors.
ideas.earned_secret: A co-op's constraint is not money, because RUS and CFC lend. It is crews. The manager who calls three contractors in February gets none until October, and contractors say yes to anyone who can commit crew-months a year ahead.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign a G&T or association sponsor; compile a 36-month pipeline from 10 co-ops; issue an RFP for reserved crew-months and collect bids; settle the legal form and the lead agency.

ideas.title: Pre-Accepted Substations for non-hyperscaler load
ideas.one_liner: Sell developers of 20-300 MW campuses a customer-owned substation and gen-tie package designed in advance to their utility's standard, with equipment slots reserved, so interconnection takes 12-15 months instead of 24-36.
ideas.customer: Neoclouds, colocation firms, powered-land developers, converted miners and industrial reshoring projects with signed will-serve letters, outside the top six hyperscalers. First 10: sites in ERCOT, AEP and Dominion territory, Georgia and Arizona.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Developer's Chief Development Officer or VP Infrastructure from site power capex (my estimate $30-70k/MW for the customer-owned scope), often with lender sign-off.
ideas.problem: Above about 10 MW the operator typically designs, builds and maintains its own substation (core equipment $3-7M, total interconnection $20-100M+, vendor estimates). These buyers lack in-house utility engineering. Each utility has its own standards for relay schemes, SCADA, bus configurations, clearances and metering; designs get rejected or reworked for months, and transformers at 128 weeks must be ordered before design settles. Study fees of $100-300k and $50k/MW security in Texas's draft rule, FERC's June 2026 show-cause orders and 768 GW of phantom load raise the cost of slipping.
ideas.solution: A library of 25-30 utilities' customer-owned-substation requirements compiled into rules; 4-6 pre-engineered families (100/200/300 MW, ring or breaker-and-a-half, 115-230 kV) with utility-reviewed one-lines and protection schemes; reserved transformer slots with two or three makers (Spec Passport); factory-built control houses; construction by accredited crews scheduled with Ready-to-Build; a utility acceptance package. Revenue is a design/management fee of 8-10% plus margin on procurement and EPC, booked gross.
ideas.why_now: WoodMac's split (12% firm, 17% likely, rest phantom) means only real projects need execution, and developers with firm service cannot wait for custom engineering; interconnection collateral and study fees make delay expensive.
ideas.wedge: Three 100-150 MW sites with signed will-serve letters in one utility territory as proofs.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption: WoodMac's roughly 28% serveable of 1,066 GW is about 300 GW over 6-8 years = 30-45 GW a year; about 40% outside the top-six hyperscalers = 12-18 GW; at $50k/MW for the customer-owned scope = $0.6-0.9B (up to $1-2B with gen-ties). $100M gross is 5-10% of that, at a net margin of 10-15%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Quanta, MYR, Burns & McDonnell, Black & Veatch, Sargent & Lundy, POWER Engineers; Hitachi Energy, Siemens Energy and GE Vernova turnkey; Powell and Eaton e-houses; Unlimited Industries (a16z, $12M seed; claims pre-construction engineering cut from six months to weeks); Tiros; hyperscalers in-house.
ideas.why_they_lose: EPC majors are capacity-limited and favor large programs; OEMs sell equipment, not utility acceptance; AI-native EPCs optimize layouts but do not hold 30 utilities' acceptance rules. Risks: utilities change standards, Unlimited builds the same library.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (pre-approvals and equipment slots) plus process power.
ideas.earned_secret: The substation is rarely late because of engineering. It is late because the utility's standards group rejects it on page 140 of its own standard, after the transformer is already on order.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick two utilities' standards and compile them; draw the 100 and 200 MW families; get an informal utility pre-review; reserve transformer slots; sign LOIs with three developers.

ideas.title: Make-Ready Rail: the bulk pole-application exchange
ideas.one_liner: Be the single bulk-application, loading-analysis, estimating and make-ready rail between telecom attachers and about 2,000 pole-owning utilities, paid per pole by the attacher, so FCC shot clocks are met and fiber gets built.
ideas.customer: Fiber and cable attachers, BEAD subgrantees and their contractors; pole-owning utilities that cannot meet the clock. First 10: six BEAD-funded regional ISPs in California, two cable operators, two co-ops that own poles.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The attacher's VP Network Engineering or Construction, from the make-ready and engineering line of build capex (industry range $500-5,000 per pole).
ideas.problem: The FCC's 2025-07-25 order sets 90-day surveys, 29-day estimates and 120/180-day make-ready, and requires bulk applications; BEAD builds touch about 3.9M utility-owned poles across 2,053 electric utilities (ACLP, May 2026); California providers have waited a year or more (CPUC D.26-05-007). Each utility has its own application format, survey method and fees (CPS Energy: $2 review, $25 loading analysis, $55-64 make-ready engineering per pole), and the pole desk is a handful of people whose fees do not fund hiring.
ideas.solution: One bulk package (KMZ/GIS routes) normalized to each owner's form, with loading analyses by licensed engineers; field data from utility-approved contractors under the FCC's self-help provisions; make-ready estimates from each owner's unit-price schedule; every pole tracked against its FCC clock with a complaint-ready evidence package; dispatch of utility-approved crews for communications-space make-ready. The asset is a 'pole truth' database: survey once, reuse for the next attacher, the utility and insurers.
ideas.why_now: FCC order (2025), FCC 26-6 definitions (2026), BEAD, AT&T and Verizon each above 10% of Dycom's revenue, Dycom FY2027 backlog about $12B (one aggregator).
ideas.wedge: California bulk applications for 20-50k poles for three to five BEAD subgrantees.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assumption: pole-related cost averages about $320 per BEAD pole ($1.25B / 3.9M) and up to $1,190. Net fee model at about $80 per pole (review, loading analysis, engineering, management) needs 1.25M poles a year; I estimate 6-12M poles a year need attachment applications (BEAD about 1M a year plus AT&T, Verizon/Frontier, Lumen, Charter/Cox and regional builds, all unverified), so that is 10-20% of poles. Gross booking of make-ready field work reaches $100M at roughly 170-300k poles (3-5%) but nets about 15%.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Utilities' own desks and engineering vendors (Osmose, Katapult-type loading software; not verified), telecom contractors Dycom, MasTec and Quanta, and attachers' in-house teams. ikeGPS PoleForeman reached about NZ$11M ARR in two years (secondary source), showing demand for pole software. I found no funded startup doing bulk make-ready.
ideas.why_they_lose: Utilities cannot standardize across each other; attachers each solve it alone; contractors are paid for field work and prefer fewer, bigger crews.
ideas.moat: Network economies (once the major owners accept the rail, attachers must use it) plus a cornered resource (the pole database).
ideas.earned_secret: Pole owners are not stonewalling. Their pole desk has four people and the survey fee does not cover a loading analysis. Hand them a complete, engineered application and the clock starts working for you.
ideas.first_90_days: Take three BEAD subgrantees' routes in California and file 20k-pole bulk applications with two PE firms running loading analyses; track every pole against the FCC clock and publish cycle times.

ideas.title: Shop Ledger: cross-shop carrier-health network, paid in 24 hours
ideas.one_liner: A neutral credit network across independent heavy-duty shops that sees every shop's invoices to a carrier plus the carrier's ELD activity, so shops get paid in 24 hours and healthy carriers get net-45 terms.
ideas.customer: Independent heavy-duty shops with 5-30 technicians and more than $250k a year of fleet receivables, and the carriers with 5-200 trucks they bill. First 10: shops in one metro (for example Dallas-Fort Worth) already running Fullbay or ShopView.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Shop pays a 2.0% discount on guaranteed invoices (replaces fleet-card merchant fees, bad debt and its own factoring line); carrier pays 1.0% for net-45 (replaces card fees and late-pay penalties). Signers: shop owner or controller; carrier owner or maintenance manager. Budget line exists: ShopView describes shops fronting about $15k for 60 days and fleets on net-30 to net-90.
ideas.problem: Shops are the unsecured lenders to trucking in the third year of a freight recession, and each shop sees only its own invoices so it cannot tell whether a carrier is slow everywhere. Existing tools move money (Fullbay Payments, RoadSync) or buy invoices on application-based credit (cbCharge); none watches the carrier. Fullbay/Stripe survey: 31% of operators delay repairs for cash-flow reasons.
ideas.solution: Shops connect their shop software; carriers consent to ELD data (miles, engine hours, idle days) via Samsara or Motive APIs. A cross-shop payment-behavior ledger plus ELD activity yields a daily carrier-health score. The network guarantees payment in 24 hours on invoices to carriers above a threshold; carriers get net-45 and repay by sweep from their factor, fuel card or settlement. Later add dealers and distributors with their small-fleet receivables.
ideas.why_now: Third year of the freight recession and R&M up 8.6% in 2025 (ATRI). ELD vendors now expose APIs and launched maintenance products (Motive Aug 2026, Samsara), so live carrier data is available for the first time. Fullbay built acceptance rails but its own survey shows credit is the missing layer.
ideas.wedge: 10 shops in one metro, invoices under $5k from carriers with 12+ months of ELD history, 2% for 24-hour pay, free for shops to join.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Blended take 3.0% (2.0% shop + 1.0% carrier) needs $3.3B of financed invoices a year. Outsourced repair and parts spend is about $50B (A: ~half of the $100B pool; ATRI says 5-25 truck fleets do ~48% in-house), so ~6.6% of outsourced spend, with losses held under ~1% of volume. Fullbay's claimed $5.04B of annual shop billing shows one network can carry that scale. Share needed is heroic (6-7%); mark as a companion to the Uptime Plan and Pay-by-the-Mile.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Fullbay Payments (Stripe; ACH, cards, Affirm/Klarna BNPL, next-day funding); RoadSync (embedded fleet-card/ACH acceptance, Fullbay partner since 2022); cbCharge/Corporate Billing (pays shop within 24h on its own credit decision); TruckSuite/Repair ACES (2021 no-recourse customer repair financing); fleet-card networks WEX/EFS/Comdata/T-Chek; freight factors serve carriers not shops (from memory: Triumph, RTS, Apex). Hidden-incumbent risk: Fullbay (Mainsail/JMI) owns the shop record and can add credit.
ideas.why_they_lose: Fullbay sees only its own shops and is a software vendor avoiding balance-sheet risk (unverified); cbCharge and TruckSuite underwrite on applications not live ELD; fleet cards give payment but at merchant fees and no carrier credit judgment; factors finance freight bills, not repair bills.
ideas.moat: Network effects on data (cross-shop payment behavior plus ELD makes the score better with every shop), plus scale economies in funding cost and switching costs once a shop's cash flow depends on 24-hour pay.
ideas.earned_secret: A shop knows a carrier is dying three weeks before the bank does: PM visits stop, trucks stop moving, last invoices are paid on a spouse's card. One shop sees one slice; a network joining invoice behavior with ELD miles sees the whole curve (backtest on 50 failed carriers before believing).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 10 shops; get 24 months of anonymized AR history from each to backtest the score; get ELD consent from 100 carriers; open a $3-5M warehouse line; clear commercial-finance licensing and disclosure laws (California, New York and others) with counsel.

ideas.title: Overnight Yard Crews: Level-1 PM and tire crews with remote master techs
ideas.one_liner: Fix the technician shortage by changing the job: train hourly Level-1 crews in weeks to do checklist work (PM, inspections, tires, brakes, lights) in the fleet's own yard at night, with a Level-3 master tech on video for escalations.
ideas.customer: Fleets with 50-2,000 trucks and a yard (private fleets, food distributors, waste, school and transit) that cannot staff in-house shops, plus OEMs needing recall and campaign capacity. First 10: yards within 60 miles of one metro hub with PM backlogs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Fleet PM, inspection and tire budget at ~$115/hour (A) versus dealer shop rates of ~$140-$195 (unverified); signer: director or VP of maintenance. Second payer: OEM warranty and campaign budget (pool claims $3.94B a year; Daimler already pays Love's for campaign work).
ideas.problem: ATRI: 65.5% of diesel shops understaffed and 19.3% of positions unfilled; 61.8% of techs enter untrained and cost 357 hours and $8,211 of trainee wages; 44% consider leaving. Dealer technicians are paid flat-rate so low-ticket PM and tire work backs up; truck stops are fixed-site and fixed-hours; apprentices get junk work.
ideas.solution: Standard-work crews of two Level-1 workers in a branded van or at the customer's bays, run to a checklist per service, with a Level-3 mentor on video and a parts kit pre-loaded from the ELD PM schedule. Hourly pay not flat-rate; 4-6 week training; apprenticeship ladder to Level-3 so the crew is also the pipeline. Partner with community colleges so short programs can qualify for Workforce Pell from 2027.
ideas.why_now: 2025 ATRI shortage data; Workforce Pell (July 2026) and the apprenticeship order (Apr 2025) put public money behind short programs; data-center generator work pays $37-$42/hour (one posting) and pulls experienced techs away; Daimler/Love's ExpressPoint proves OEMs buy non-dealer capacity.
ideas.wedge: Overnight PM and DOT annual inspections for 10 yards, then tires and brakes, then OEM campaigns.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) A crew-year bills ~$345k (2 techs x 1,500 billable hours x $115). $100M needs ~290 crews, ~600 field staff and ~60 master-tech mentors. If checklist labor (PM, inspection, tires, brakes, lighting) is ~$35B (A, ~40% of pool labor and parts-labor), that is ~0.3% of it. Demand is not the constraint; hiring and route density are.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Ryder (Torque by Ryder mobile PM in six states, SelectCare); Love's Speedco (1,500+ bays, company claim); Penske contract maintenance (133,700 customer-owned vehicles); dealer mobile units (Allegiance, Bergey's, Vanguard); Valvoline heavy-duty fleet service; FleetPride/TruckPro service centers and mobile; TDI Fleet Services; Diesel Laptops remote virtual diesel tech (since 2019); True North Fleet Services (PE roll-up). Assume all of them.
ideas.why_they_lose: Dealer flat-rate pay makes PM the work nobody wants (unverified); OEMs cannot run service (franchise laws, unverified); truck stops cannot move to the customer's yard; Ryder's mobile offer is retail-priced and in six states. Nobody has made Level-1 work a trained, hourly, standardized job with a ladder.
ideas.moat: Process power (training standard, checklists, QA) and a cornered resource (apprentice pipeline, instructor bench), with route-density scale economies. Weak against Ryder and Love's scale, so the standard should be licensable to shops.
ideas.earned_secret: The shortage is partly task allocation: maybe half of billable hours at a typical shop are checklist work (Fullbay line shares suggest but do not prove it). Apprenticeships fail because apprentices get the junk work; make that work the first job and the best self-select upward.
ideas.first_90_days: Hire two ex-instructors and a recruiter; write the 20 standard-work cards (PM-A, DOT annual, brake relines, tires, lights); pilot 3 yards of one regional fleet; apply with a community-college partner for Workforce Pell eligibility (needs 12-month track record plus governor and federal approval).

ideas.title: Pay-by-the-Mile: major-repair credit repaid through the factor and the odometer
ideas.one_liner: Finance the $2,500-$40,000 engine, transmission and aftertreatment repairs owner-operators and small fleets cannot pay for, collect in cents per mile through the freight factor or settlement they already use, with the odometer as the schedule.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators and sub-20-truck fleets (97% of fleets per FMCSA 2019) with 3+ years in business and thin credit. First 10: 100 borrowers from 5 independent shops already using Fullbay Payments.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Borrower pays ~12-18% APR-equivalent plus fees; shop pays a 2% merchant fee to be paid at completion. Signer: the owner-operator or small-fleet owner; the budget line is the repair reserve they lack (31% delay repairs for cash flow).
ideas.problem: Fullbay/Stripe: 61% would likely use pay-over-time and interest is 61% for major engine repairs, but only 30% of shops offer a plan and 13% can use third-party financing. BNPL tickets are small and consumer-grade underwriting declines thin-file commercial borrowers. A parked owner-operator loses ~$700/day (unverified).
ideas.solution: Underwrite on ELD miles, tenure and repair history, not FICO. Repay by sweep from the borrower's factor or broker settlement before the remainder is released, with a per-mile accrual from the ELD as trigger. Collateral: lien on truck and replaced component, and a start-inhibit only when parked, never while moving. Shop paid at completion. Later finance donor-truck engine swaps from Second Source.
ideas.why_now: R&M +8.6% in 2025 (ATRI); tariffs add 20-30% to heavy parts; trucks held longer; the Fullbay/Stripe survey quantifies demand; Motive and Samsara made ELD data portable.
ideas.wedge: One freight factor with ~500 small-carrier clients as the sweep partner; 50 pilot loans up to $10k.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Revenue ~14% of originations (11% interest + 3% fees) so $715M of originations. Pool: ~1.2M trucks in small fleets x 0.35 repairs over $2,500 a year x $8,000 = ~$3.4B, so 21% of all such repairs must be financed. Heroic; credit losses of 5-8% of originations must be absorbed. A companion to Shop Ledger, not a standalone venture-scale bet.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Fullbay Payments with Stripe (Affirm/Klarna); TruckSuite/Repair ACES (non-recourse customer financing); cbCharge; freight factors that already hold the borrower's cash flow and advance fuel (from memory: Triumph, RTS, Apex, Thunder Funding, OTR Solutions); general SMB lenders; Mudflap's fuel card ($50M Series B 2022). A factor adding repair advances is the likeliest competitor.
ideas.why_they_lose: BNPL has consumer-grade underwriting and small limits; factors do not finance repairs or talk to shops (unverified); shops cannot underwrite; nobody sits in the repayment waterfall and holds the ELD feed at once.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (sweep agreements with factors and brokers) plus counter-positioning against BNPL and scale economies in funding cost; data improves pricing over time.
ideas.earned_secret: Repayment is the product: a trucker paid through a factor repays the factor first, so a lender inside that waterfall sees losses near factor loss rates while an unsecured small-business loan to the same person loses several times more (unverified; test with a pilot).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one factor and 5 shops; build the ELD mileage trigger; $5M warehouse line; counsel on state commercial-financing disclosure laws (California, New York and others), usury, UCC lien priority against the factor, and immobilization liability.

ideas.title: Warranty Wrapper: the OEM-paid multi-brand network for non-dealer warranty and campaign work
ideas.one_liner: Be the contract vehicle between OEM warranty budgets and the independent shops, fleet in-house shops and mobile crews that can do warranty and recall work faster than dealers, carrying authorization, training, prior approval, parts return and claims compliance.
ideas.customer: OEM warranty and aftermarket directors (Daimler Truck NA, Volvo/Mack, PACCAR, Navistar/International and component makers); fleets use the network free. First: one OEM that lacks a Love's-style partner.
ideas.payer_and_signer: OEM warranty administration budget; signer: VP of warranty or customer quality. The line is real: US heavy-duty manufacturers paid $3.94B of claims in 2025 (WARRANTYWEEK) and PACCAR alone paid $772.1M (10-K).
ideas.problem: Dealer bays are full, so recalls, campaigns and light warranty work wait while trucks sit. Daimler's answer was one exclusive partner (Love's, 400+ truck-stop locations, Freightliner ExpressPoint). OEMs cannot own service (franchise laws, unverified) and fleets with in-house shops cannot get paid for warranty work they could do.
ideas.solution: Onboard shops and fleet shops as authorized providers with OEM-specific training and tooling; digital prior approval; standard three-C narrative and photo capture; parts-return logistics; first-pass claim filing and appeals. OEM sets labor rates; platform keeps ~10% of pass-through. Fleet-side software (Samsara drafts claims) pushes more claims in; this is the provider-side rail.
ideas.why_now: Daimler/Love's precedent proven since Jan 2024; claims at $3.94B; EPA July 2026 proposal keeps emissions warranty at 5 years/100,000 miles so OEMs keep cost-per-claim pressure; telematics vendors adding claim drafting raise claim volume from fleets.
ideas.wedge: One OEM campaign: 200 trucks at five fleet yards in one region, with the local dealer signing off and keeping parts and claim filing as in the Love's model.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) $1.0B of pass-through (25% of the $3.94B claims pool) at a 10% net take is $100M; if booked gross, $100M is only 2.5% of claims. Net basis is heroic and needs at least two OEMs to open their programs. Report net; gross overstates economics.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Franchised dealers (primary); Love's Truck Care/Speedco for Freightliner; OEM warranty portals; Samsara (fleet-side claim drafting, dependent on OEM terms); dealer-side warranty administrators (from memory). Love's said it was not approved for warranty or campaign work before the Daimler deal.
ideas.why_they_lose: Dealers' territorial franchises and full bays cap capacity; Love's covers truck stops and one OEM; OEMs cannot run service; fleets cannot get paid. Nobody runs a multi-brand authorization-and-claims rail for non-dealer providers.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (OEM system integration and provider authorizations), process power (first-pass claim acceptance rate), and network coverage.
ideas.earned_secret: A dealer warranty administrator knows 8-12% of claims get short-paid or charged back (unverified) and that campaign work is scheduled last because it pays flat time with no upside; OEMs measure campaign completion and will pay for speed. Whoever gets clean claims accepted first pass becomes the preferred vendor.
ideas.first_90_days: Hire an ex-dealer warranty administrator and an ex-OEM field-service manager; pitch Volvo/Mack and PACCAR with the Love's precedent; run the 200-truck pilot; build the claim-acceptance dashboard; check state dealer-franchise laws on OEMs using non-franchisees.

ideas.title: Uptime Plan: cost-per-mile maintenance for the fleet the lessors and OEMs ignore
ideas.one_liner: A fixed price per mile for PM, wear items and covered repairs at any shop in a network, for mixed-make trucks in fleets of 3-50, underwritten from ELD data and repair history and backed by an insurer.
ideas.customer: Owner-operators and fleets of 3-50 trucks running 6-15-year-old mixed-make equipment. First 10: fleets of 10-30 trucks in one metro, sourced from independent shops and an ELD vendor's partner list.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The fleet's maintenance budget (R&M plus tires averages 26.5 cents/mile in ATRI 2025; an HDMA study reports ~25 cents for owner-operators, definitions differ). Signer: owner or fleet manager. A fixed price replaces a variance they carry today.
ideas.problem: OEM programs (Volvo Cost Per Mile, Daimler Extended OPTIMUM) are single-brand and route to dealers. Ryder SelectCare and Penske contract maintenance need their own shop density and are priced for larger accounts. Third-party plans (National Truck Protection) cover breakdowns on used trucks, not PM. Telematics vendors will not carry risk.
ideas.solution: Price each truck by age band, duty cycle and ELD fault history; network of independent shops and mobile crews paid in 24 hours (pairs with Shop Ledger); PM compliance and fault alerts as conditions; insurer or reinsurer holds the risk; a roadside desk. Plans range from PM-only to PM plus covered repairs.
ideas.why_now: Fleets holding trucks longer, R&M +8.6% in 2025; EPA July 2026 proposal keeps emissions warranty at 5 years/100,000 miles so fleets carry aftertreatment risk after 100,000 miles; tariffs added 20-30% to heavy parts; ELD data is now portable and shops sit on Fullbay; the 2021-23 truck cohort (2022 Class 8 retail 309,615, ACT) has left basic coverage.
ideas.wedge: PM plus roadside plus tires for 6-15-year-old trucks in fleets of 10-30, with a capped repair add-on, at ~14 cents/mile.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Average price 17 cents x 75,000 miles = $12,750 a truck-year; platform keeps 22% (fees, shop spread, float) = $2,805. $100M needs ~35,600 trucks: 0.9% of 3.8M Class 8 (TruckNews) or ~2% of ~1.7M small-fleet trucks (A), and 27% of Penske's 133,700 customer-owned vehicles under contract maintenance (10-K FY2025). If booked gross as obligor, ~7,800 trucks. Needs reinsurance capital and a loss ratio near 78% (A).
ideas.who_does_it_today: Penske (133,700 customer-owned vehicles); Ryder SelectCare and Torque; NationaLease (140+ independent lessors, 900 locations); Volvo Cost Per Mile; Daimler Extended OPTIMUM and other OEM plans; National Truck Protection and similar third parties (3,000+ garages); Love's/Speedco; ELD vendors give alerts only. Hidden-incumbent risk is high: a lessor offering a mixed-make any-shop tier is the obvious counter.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs earn ~24% pretax on parts (PACCAR 2025) and a multi-brand independent-shop plan cannibalizes it; Ryder and Penske profit from owned-shop utilization and cover only where they own bays; NTP covers breakdowns not maintenance on one segment; telematics vendors do not carry risk or run shops.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against OEM and lessor economics, scale economies in shop rates and parts, and a cornered data set (ELD plus repair history per truck).
ideas.earned_secret: Maintenance cost per truck is far more predictable than small fleets believe once age band and duty cycle are controlled; they pay a no-scale premium (HDMA 25 cents vs ATRI 21.5 cents suggests ~15%, on different bases) because nobody will take the variance (unverified; backtest 5,000 truck-years).
ideas.first_90_days: Hire an actuary who priced contract maintenance; backtest 5,000 truck-years from Fullbay or ELD partners; secure an MGA/fronting arrangement and a reinsurer; sign 20 independent shops and a mobile partner; enroll 10 fleets. Legal check: service-contract versus insurance classification by state (California's definition reportedly excludes 30,000-lb GVWR and up, secondary, verify); use insurer-backed paper from day one.

ideas.title: Public Fleet Bench: fixed-fee maintenance for fleets that cannot pay market wages
ideas.one_liner: Sell school districts, transit agencies, counties and refuse haulers a fixed per-vehicle maintenance contract delivered by market-wage crews inside their own garages, because their pay scales guarantee they cannot hire.
ideas.customer: School transportation directors (~480,000 buses), county and municipal fleet managers, refuse and public-works fleets. First 10: districts of 300-1,500 buses with mechanic vacancies above 30% (for example in North Carolina, Georgia and Texas).
ideas.payer_and_signer: District or county operations budget (fleet maintenance and contract services); signer: chief operations officer, fleet director, or the board via a cooperative purchasing contract. Many districts' diesel costs run 6-20% over budget (2026 AASA survey), squeezing headcount.
ideas.problem: Guilford County Schools is ~14 mechanics short (roughly half strength) with 600 buses; Charlotte-Mecklenburg had 17 vacancies of 47 and 27% of 108 inspected buses had serious defects (2023). Districts cannot raise one job class without ripple effects and union scales (unverified). Turnkey transport contractors want the whole route contract, which districts resist (unverified).
ideas.solution: Fixed annual fee per vehicle for PM, state inspections and repairs, delivered by Level-1/Level-3 crews (Yard Crews model) using the district's bays, parts contracts and a data dashboard. Sell PM and inspection first, then full repair.
ideas.why_now: 36% of surveyed districts short of maintenance staff; diesel overruns; retirements (trade commentary: boomers 40-50% of technicians, retiring by 2030); safety and liability exposure after failed inspections.
ideas.wedge: PM and inspection contracts below the competitive-bid threshold, delivered in the district garage.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) School bus maintenance ~$5,500/bus (STN reader survey, undated), so $100M is ~18,200 buses, 3.8% of 480,000: roughly 45 districts of 400 buses. Public pool ~$5B a year (school buses $2.6B plus transit, refuse, public works), so $100M is ~2% of the pool or ~8% of an assumed 25% contracted share. Refuse trucks cost far more per vehicle and widen the path.
ideas.who_does_it_today: District in-house garages; turnkey transport operators bundling drivers and maintenance (First Student, Student Transportation of America, National Express, from memory); transit contract managers (Transdev, MV, from memory); dealer service departments; Ryder public-sector fleet business (from memory). I found no named maintenance-only specialist.
ideas.why_they_lose: Districts cannot pay market wages or hire seasonally; turnkey operators want the whole route; dealers are capacity-bound; nobody sells a maintenance-only fixed fee with an SLA.
ideas.moat: Switching costs and procurement incumbency (past performance, cooperative contract vehicles), plus process power from the shared crew model.
ideas.earned_secret: A district fleet director would rather outsource PM and inspections than drivers: the vacancy is permanent, the board cannot pay more for one job class, and every failed inspection is a headline (unverified; test with 10 directors).
ideas.first_90_days: Hire a retired district fleet director to sell; answer 3 live RFPs; offer a free fleet-condition audit to 10 districts; hire 6 technicians in one county; check state procurement thresholds, prevailing-wage and union no-subcontracting clauses.

ideas.title: Second Source: graded, warrantied used and reman power-train parts plus a core exchange
ideas.one_liner: Become the default 30-60%-below-new answer to the tariff: dismantle donor trucks, buy cores from shops with instant pay, test and grade every engine, transmission, turbo, ECM and injector set to a published standard, and sell with a 12-month warranty.
ideas.customer: Independent shops and small fleets facing 20-30% price increases on heavy components. First 10: 10 shops within 100 miles of the first donor yard.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The shop or fleet parts budget; signer: shop owner or fleet maintenance manager. A price-for-quality swap inside an existing line.
ideas.problem: Reman parts run 30-70% below new (FreightWaves, May 2026) and outperform the broader parts market, but independents lack trusted grading and warranties on used units; OEM reman is dealer-routed with OEM-controlled cores; salvage yards are local and ungraded; shops scrap cores. Distributors reprice preemptively and do not itemize tariffs.
ideas.solution: Buy donor trucks (auctions, failed carriers, total losses) and cores from shops at grade-based prices; bench or dyno test and grade A/B/C with a published standard; reman high-value units; catalog and API into shop systems; core exchange with instant credit. Aftertreatment is handled separately in the Aftertreatment Exchange.
ideas.why_now: 25% Section 232 tariffs from Nov 2025; injectors, turbos, EGR, DPF assemblies and transmissions +20-30% (Decisiv/TMC); steel and aluminum duties at 50%; USMCA parts exemption conditional and the US declined to renew USMCA on July 1 2026; 2025 new-truck sales down 13.4% (208,155) keep older trucks running and stressed carriers produce donors; Cummins-Meritor ($3.7B) and Dorman-Dayton ($338M) show HD aftermarket assets being re-rated.
ideas.wedge: Five SKU families: ECMs, injector sets, turbochargers, EGR coolers, transmissions and axles.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) If used plus reman is ~8% of the $37B parts pool today ($3.0B) and rises to ~12% on the tariff ($4.4B), $100M is ~2.3% of that. Operationally ~83,000 units at $1,200, from ~5,500 donor trucks at ~$18k of sellable parts each plus cores bought from shops. Constraint is core supply and test capacity, not demand.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEM reman through dealers (Cummins, Detroit, PACCAR, Volvo/Mack, from memory); Dorman (Dayton Parts); Cummins-Meritor; independent rebuilders; salvage yards such as TLG Trucks (25 acres, 200+ salvage trucks per its site); FleetPride/TruckPro reman lines; HDA Truck Pride members. I found no national graded-component standard.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs and dealers earn ~24% pretax on parts (PACCAR) and run closed core loops; distributors push private label and import lines; salvage yards cannot warrant or grade; nobody holds both supply (cores, donors) and trust (grade plus warranty).
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (core and donor supply contracts) plus brand/standard (grading data and warranty experience) and scale economies in test equipment.
ideas.earned_secret: Cores, not demand, are the scarce input; every shop has a core pile out back. A dyno-tested, warrantied used unit is worth ~70% of reman price; the missing piece is a grade the shop trusts (unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Lease a yard; buy 20 donor trucks; hire a dyno-capable test lead; publish the grading card; sign 10 shops on core-exchange credit. Legal check: EPA remanufacturing and emission-certification rules for rebuilt engines (40 CFR 1068.120, unverified), salvage-title and hazardous-waste rules.

ideas.title: Aftertreatment Exchange: pooled, multi-brand DPF/DOC/SCR swap units
ideas.one_liner: A national pool of cleaned, flow-tested aftertreatment units shipped to any shop in 4 hours at a flat exchange price, so the truck leaves in hours instead of waiting two days for cleaning.
ideas.customer: Independent shops, mobile mechanics and fleet in-house shops. First 10: 10 shops near Dallas and Atlanta with 20+ aftertreatment events a month.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Shop or fleet aftertreatment budget; signer: shop owner or maintenance manager. Cleaning costs $350-$600 and replacement $4,800-$8,200 (vendor sources); the swap sits between them.
ideas.problem: OEM exchange programs (Detroit at 800+ locations, Volvo/Mack reman) are brand-specific and dealer-routed; independent cleaners work one unit at a time and the truck waits. The 2027 NOx standard stays and the July 2026 EPA proposal keeps emissions warranty at 5 years/100,000 miles, so cost stays with fleets. Platinum $1,793, palladium $1,299, rhodium $8,550 an ounce (Aug 21 2026) make failed units valuable and theft attractive.
ideas.solution: Regional hubs with bake, air, aqueous cleaning and flow-bench testing; rotating inventory per hub; exchange at a flat price with a 12-month warranty; telematics regen data to trigger swaps before failure; PGM recovery on failed units; ash disposal.
ideas.why_now: 2027 NOx standard unchanged; July 2026 NPRM leaves warranty at 100,000 miles; 6.6-year Class 8 trade cycles and 12.8-year average fleet age (KPMG) push more trucks into the failure window; metals prices. Counter-risk: the same proposal drops DEF derates, which may cut forced shop visits.
ideas.wedge: DPF and DOC swaps for the top 20 engine families in two metros.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) ~5.3M DPF-equipped Class 6-8 trucks x 0.35 cleanings a year x $450 = $0.83B, plus 4% replacements x $5,500 = $1.17B, about $2.0B in total. $100M is ~5% of that. Pool capital: ~20,000 units in circulation x $1,500 = $30M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: OEM exchange and reman programs (Detroit 800+ locations, Volvo/Mack since 2008); Cummins/Fleetguard (not verified); local DPF cleaning shops and mobile cleaners; FleetPride/TruckPro and HDA members selling new and reman units (not verified). I found no national multi-brand pooled exchange, but the search was thin.
ideas.why_they_lose: OEMs sell new aftertreatment at $4.8k-$8.2k and run exchange through dealers; local cleaners have no pooled inventory; distributors sell units, not turnaround time.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in cleaning labs and pooled-asset density (delivery time), plus a cornered resource in core supply.
ideas.earned_secret: The money is turnaround time, not cleaning: fleets pay thousands to avoid two days of downtime, and a swap takes cleaning off the critical path (unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Build one lab; buy 2,000 cores; sign 10 shops; log flow-bench data on every unit; check EPA and CARB treatment of remanufactured aftertreatment (CARB Executive Order requirements, unverified), hazardous-waste rules for ash and catalyst, and tampering risk.

ideas.title: Clock-Out Capital: visit-level Medicaid finance priced on recoupment
ideas.one_liner: Buy each EVV-verified Medicaid visit the day it happens, pay the aide that night and the agency by morning, and price it on whether it will be clawed back, not on how old the invoice is.
ideas.customer: Medicaid personal care agencies with $3-20M of annual Medicaid billings that live on factoring lines or personally guaranteed bank lines. First 10 picked from the HHS provider-level Medicaid file (T1019 billers paying $300k+ a month and growing) in NY, PA, IL, NJ and FL, plus referrals from two home care billing firms and one state association.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The agency, from the interest and factoring-fee line it already pays (reported 18-36% effective annual rates, unverified) and the payroll-processing line. Signer is the agency owner/CEO or CFO.
ideas.problem: Aides are paid weekly but Medicaid or the MCO pays 30-60 days later, and an EVV mismatch or authorization gap restarts the clock. Lenders underwrite the agency's aging report, but the real loss is a payer clawing back or denying a visit months later over an EVV, authorization, eligibility or exclusion-list problem.
ideas.solution: Ingest visits from the EVV vendor plus authorizations and daily eligibility. Run a five-point visit check (units left, eligibility that day, EVV match, caregiver exclusion screen, valid rate and modifier). Advance 85-90% against passing visits into a lockbox in the agency's name under a control agreement. Pay aides through a payroll rail the next morning (agency stays employer). Release the reserve when the payer pays. Target 12-16% annualized for clean visits. Fund from specialty credit funds, later asset-backed notes; a payer-anchored approved-payables version is the scale path.
ideas.why_now: CMS scrutiny of personal care since Feb 2026 and state moves to enforce EVV matches slow and shrink payments (the NY edit that blocks unmatched claims existed but was off). HHAX put payroll on EVV data (CarePay, Aug 2026) but has no balance sheet. The Feb 2026 public HHS provider-level file lets a new lender screen every biller. MCOs now adjudicate most Medicaid claims.
ideas.wedge: $1-2M advances to 10 agencies in one or two states, sold as 'paid on clock-out' payroll bridging; the visit-level loss data is the asset.
ideas.path_to_100m: Gross revenue at 15% annualized needs about $667M average balance, about $4.9B of visits funded a year at a 50-day turn (arithmetic). That is about 10% of the $46.4B personal-care pool or 3.8% of the $129.4B HCBS total; about 700 agencies at $7M financed each (HHAX alone connects 30K+ agencies). Share needed: about 10% of personal care, heroic. Pre-tax margin is roughly 10-20% of gross revenue, so $100M of revenue is $10-20M of profit; it is a balance-sheet business. Payroll fees add under $5M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Alleon Healthcare Capital (85% advance on a NY home care facility), eCapital (markets HCBS receivable lines), bank asset-based lines, small-business lenders advertising payroll bridges, HHAeXchange (payroll plus earned-wage access, no agency financing found). No venture-funded home-care-specific lender found, but only 3 searches on this.
ideas.why_they_lose: Factors price the agency (aging, concentration, personal guarantee) and cannot see the five visit-level checks; banks won't do $1M lines on payer-assigned paper; HHAX is paid by payers, has no balance sheet and cannot lend against its own customers' payers; earned-wage vendors advance the aide's pay from the employer's cash, not against the invoice.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (visit-level loss data by payer, agency and exception code plus lockbox relationships) and scale economies in funding cost; switching costs once the payroll rail is in.
ideas.earned_secret: In Medicaid personal care the credit risk is not the payer defaulting; it is recoupment and denial found months later. A visit that passes five checks is far safer paper than a 30-day-old invoice from a clean-looking agency. (Unverified insider claim; replay 12 months of 10 agencies' visits to test.)
ideas.first_90_days: Get EVV exports from 10 agencies; build the five-check engine; replay 12 months of their visits to measure denials and recoupments; line up a $5M warehouse from a specialty lender; retain healthcare-finance counsel for the lockbox in two states; hire an ex-HHAX or MCO provider-ops lead.

ideas.title: The exception-free fiscal intermediary
ideas.one_liner: Run statewide participant-directed payroll at about 30% under the incumbent's price by making the EVV record the timesheet and automating the exceptions that eat the call center.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid and developmental-disability agencies that buy fiscal/employer-agent services. First targets: Kentucky's participant-directed FMS RFP (proposals due Nov 6 2026), Ohio DODD's statewide FMS, and a waiver-only contract in a mid-size state.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The state, from the FMS administrative line (per participant per month, federal match applies). Signer: state Medicaid director or developmental-disabilities director, through competitive procurement.
ideas.problem: New York showed states one statewide FI can replace about 600, and claimed large savings (disputed), but also showed the state's biggest fear: aides unpaid on day one. Fixed per-member fees reward incumbents for staying labor-heavy, and only 4 of 130+ New York bidders reportedly qualified.
ideas.solution: An FI built on three rules: hours flow from EVV-approved visits straight into payroll (the timesheet is not a separate document); onboarding (I-9, W-4, new-hire, background and exclusion checks) is a tracked pipeline measured in days; every exception (missing approval, hours over budget, overtime, wrong funding source) is auto-resolved or routed with a deadline. Offer a payroll-certainty backstop: the FI fronts payroll from a credit line if the state pays late. Price $75-115 per participant per month against $98-160 reference points elsewhere.
ideas.why_now: Federal Medicaid cuts pressure state budgets; the New York precedent; live RFPs in Kentucky and Ohio; EVV aggregators now run in 29 state programs, so 'EVV equals timesheet' is feasible and fits CMS attention on EVV.
ideas.wedge: Win one small FMS contract (waiver-only or mid-size state) with a teaming partner or an acquired small FI that supplies past performance; displaced New York FIs hold staff, registrations and track records.
ideas.path_to_100m: At $1,270-1,920 per participant a year ($106-160 a month; California $160, Louisiana $105.88), $100M needs about 52,000-79,000 participants: roughly a fifth to a third of New York's 250,000, or two mid-size states. No national count of self-directing participants was found, so no national share can be stated. The book is far larger in pass-through (New York about $9B for about 250k people), but net fee per participant is what counts.
ideas.who_does_it_today: PPL (New York's sole FI), GT Independence, Acumen Fiscal Agent, Tempus Unlimited (Massachusetts); Palco and Consumer Direct Care Network also operate (from memory, unverified); NY payroll firms such as Viventium; HHAeXchange runs EVV for FI/FMS programs; Maximus was named in a New York draft.
ideas.why_they_lose: Fixed monthly fees mean any saving is the incumbent's margin, so they will not cut price; onboarding and exception handling are call-center based (unverified). In a rebid, a lower bid with a payroll-certainty backstop is a story a state director can defend.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (multi-year state contract and thousands of enrolled workers), scale economies (fixed software spread over more participants), process power in exception handling.
ideas.earned_secret: The unit of work in an FI is the exception, not the paycheck; in a legacy FI perhaps 30-40% of timesheets need a human touch (insider estimate, not sourced). A state values 'zero missed payroll' above a lower price, so the pricing wedge is the guarantee.
ideas.first_90_days: Answer the Kentucky RFP with a partner that has past performance; sign a former state FMS program manager as bid lead; build the EVV-to-payroll pipeline against one aggregator; line up a payroll backstop credit line; approach two displaced New York FIs about teaming or acquisition.

ideas.title: Proof-of-Visit: the verification rail for home care
ideas.one_liner: Sell a signed assurance score and evidence pack for every home care visit (right person, right place, no impossible overlaps), the way identity vendors sell a check per login.
ideas.customer: In order: EVV vendors that want to white-label it; MCOs and state Medicaid agencies that want to pay only provable visits; agencies and their lenders that want a verified fast lane. First 10: three agencies plus one EVV vendor on a historical replay, then one state program-integrity office.
ideas.payer_and_signer: States: EVV and program-integrity lines (federal systems match may apply, unverified); signer is the Medicaid program-integrity director. MCOs: special-investigations or payment-integrity budget; signer is the SIU head. Agencies: compliance spend. Priced at $0.30-0.80 per visit or as a savings share with a state.
ideas.problem: EVV was built as a time clock, not proof; a caregiver can tap an app or call in without being there and manual edits are invisible to the state. New York paid $14.5B of personal-care claims (44%) with no matching EVV record and the blocking edit was off; the Aug 2026 Philadelphia charges came with a federal prosecutor saying EVV was not sufficient.
ideas.solution: Layer 1 at the visit: device attestation, geofence against the service address, optional consented face match for flagged visits. Layer 2 with no hardware: a graph across everything a caregiver is paid for (overlapping visits, impossible travel, reused payroll bank accounts, billing during hospital stays or incarceration, visits under 8 minutes). Layer 3 the rail: a signed score and evidence pack via one API consumed by EVV vendors, claims engines (a pay-when-proven hard edit) and lenders. It is also the underwriting feed for the visit-finance idea.
ideas.why_now: CMS's Feb 2026 push naming personal care, the Minnesota deferral ($259.5M, more than $1B possible), the Philadelphia case, Ohio's high-risk criteria (Oct 6 2026, unverified), the NY audit and an OIG work-plan item on EVV data use. Pressure is enforcement, not a deadline that can slip. It has not happened because EVV vendors are paid per visit by states to a specification that excludes identity proof, and integrity vendors work after payment without payroll or identity data.
ideas.wedge: Historical replay for a state or MCO: run 24 months of EVV and claims through the graph, show the flagged dollars, then charge a savings share.
ideas.path_to_100m: Per-visit route: HHAX alone confirms 485M visits a year; assume 600-800M nationally. $0.40 x 250M visits = $100M, which is 30-40% of national visits, heroic. Savings-share route: New York personal care is $15.67B; at the roughly 12% improper rate in the OIG sample, about $1.9B a year; if the rail plus a hard edit avoids a quarter ($470M) and the vendor keeps 20%, about $94M from one state. Realistic path: one NY-class savings-share plus per-visit fees elsewhere. Share needed: about a third of national visits, or one New York-sized contract.
ideas.who_does_it_today: EVV vendors (HHAeXchange including Sandata, Netsmart/Tellus, Fiserv AuthentiCare, state-run portals); biometric EVV devices (state-allowed, needs a device in each home); payment-integrity vendors (Gainwell, Conduent, Cotiviti, Performant, Optum, named from background knowledge, unverified); free CMS fraud partnerships; identity vendors (Persona, ID.me, Clear) with no home care product found.
ideas.why_they_lose: EVV vendors cannot add friction for their own users or make visits fail, and are paid per visit. Integrity vendors see claims but not who was physically where. Only a party holding payroll and cross-employer data can build the cross-check.
ideas.moat: Network economies (a caregiver identity graph across states, payers and employers), counter-positioning against EVV vendors, process power.
ideas.earned_secret: Fraud sits in the last 10% of the workflow (manual edits and reason codes), and the cheapest proof is not biometrics but cross-checking a caregiver's other obligations: other employers, travel time, bank accounts. (Unverified.)
ideas.first_90_days: Replay 24 months of visits for three agencies and one EVV vendor; show flagged dollars; brief two state integrity offices; get privacy counsel on face matching; ship a non-biometric mode from day one.

ideas.title: Personal-care administrator for fee-for-service states (the NEMT-broker model)
ideas.one_liner: Take what a state buys piece by piece (assessment, authorization, network, EVV, payroll, fraud) and sell it one reconciled paid hour, the way NEMT brokers sell a managed trip.
ideas.customer: State Medicaid agencies that still run personal care fee-for-service and have a cost or fraud problem. First: one mid-size state with an RFI or waiver window.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The state, from the administrative-services line (50% federal match; 75% for certified systems operations, unverified). Signer: state Medicaid director and CFO.
ideas.problem: The assessor sets hours, the FI pays what is billed, EVV records what is clocked, the payment system pays claims, and nobody owns the reconciliation. T1019 personal-care spending rose from $9.6B to about $23.5B in six years (secondary reading of the Feb 2026 HHS file).
ideas.solution: An administrative-services contract that owns assessment scheduling and utilization review, authorizations, network enrollment, EVV-to-claims matching, fraud triage and capacity reporting for a defined population, paid a per-member monthly fee plus shared savings with a floor. It takes no delivery risk and employs no aides.
ideas.why_now: Personal-care cost trend, the NY audit, the CMS crackdown, federal attention on how states use EVV data, and ModivCare's 2025 bankruptcy clearing out the old broker story. It has not transferred because NEMT had explicit statutory brokerage authority (SSA 1902(a)(70), from memory) and a single simple unit, while personal care has free-choice rules and clinical assessment; CareBridge went to the MCO side and sold for $2.7B.
ideas.wedge: A single-function contract first (EVV-to-claims reconciliation plus utilization review for one program), then widen to the administrator role.
ideas.path_to_100m: At a 3-5% administration fee, $100M needs $2.0-3.3B of managed spend, 4-7% of the $46.4B personal-care pool. State anchors: Massachusetts PCA about $1.4B a year through one FI (from the HHS file); Missouri T1019 $6.2B across 2018-24 (secondary dashboard). So it needs two or three mid-size fee-for-service states; total fee-for-service state spend was not sourced. Share needed: about 5% of personal care, heroic, with 18-36 month cycles.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Nobody as a whole. Pieces: Maximus (New York independent assessor), Public Consulting Group and Acentra-type utilization-review vendors (unverified), HHAeXchange/Sandata (EVV), PPL and peers (FI), Gainwell and Conduent (payment systems). Only one search on the integrated model, so low confidence.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each vendor is paid per transaction (an assessment, a visit, a paycheck, a claim), so none is paid for the total bill; software vendors won't take risk.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (state systems integration) and process power; scale economies in shared analytics.
ideas.earned_secret: States leak money at handoffs between vendors; the unit a state should buy is a reconciled paid hour. (Unverified.)
ideas.first_90_days: Hire an ex-state HCBS director; pick the state; build a reconciled-hour prototype from public provider-level data plus sample EVV; form a bid team with an FI and an assessor.

ideas.title: The neutral LTSS manager for plans that compete with Elevance
ideas.one_liner: The same at-risk HCBS management CareBridge sells, owned by no health plan, for the Medicaid plans that will not hand their sickest members to a rival.
ideas.customer: Medicaid managed LTSS plans that compete with Elevance: Centene, UnitedHealthcare Community Plan, Molina, AmeriHealth Caritas, Humana, CVS/Aetna Better Health. First 10: two plans and a Blue plan with a 5,000-member shared-savings pilot in states where they run managed LTSS.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The plan, from medical-cost management or care-management vendor budgets, paid out of savings against its own HCBS and hospital trend. Signer: SVP/VP of LTSS or the Medicaid chief medical officer.
ideas.problem: The top few percent of HCBS members (long hours, missed shifts) drive a large share of spend, and a missed aide shift turns into an ED visit. Plans can't run EVV, payroll, claims and hospital data together, so they pay a vendor, and the category leader is now a competitor's subsidiary.
ideas.solution: An at-risk manager with a contractual data firewall: members' EVV, claims, admissions and payroll signals in one operating system; same-day response to missed shifts; network steering to agencies with the best continuity; fraud triage; 20% shared savings with a floor. Employs no aides.
ideas.why_now: Elevance's reported $2.7B purchase of CareBridge (closed Dec 10 2024) removed the neutral option; Elevance says it will serve all customers, which is exactly why rivals should hesitate. Federal Medicaid cuts press plan margins.
ideas.wedge: A 5,000-member pilot in one state with one plan, priced at savings only.
ideas.path_to_100m: Comparable: CareBridge served over 115,000 patients in 2023. At about $30k of managed spend per member (below the roughly $35k a year implied by the NY and MA files) and a 5% net fee, $100M needs about 67,000 at-risk members, about 58% of CareBridge's 2023 count, roughly 4% of managed-LTSS HCBS members if there are 1.5-2M (unverified).
