ideas.who_does_it_today: CareBridge (Carelon/Elevance, 17 states plus DC), plans' own LTSS teams, HHAeXchange payer network tools (software, no risk). Other care-management firms not verified.
ideas.why_they_lose: CareBridge sits inside a competing plan, so rivals' data and savings go to Elevance; HHAX takes no risk and is paid per seat; in-house teams lack integrated EVV, claims and payroll data.
ideas.moat: Switching costs, process power, and a neutrality guarantee an owned competitor can't copy.
ideas.earned_secret: Plans don't buy 'HCBS management'; they buy a lower hospital and nursing-home trend on a small, expensive cohort. (Unverified.)
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit ex-CareBridge and ex-plan LTSS leaders; pitch the plans that don't own the category; offer a firewalled pilot at savings only; use public provider files to choose states. Kill test: four of the five largest plans co-invested in CareBridge in 2022, so make three plan calls to confirm neutrality has a buyer before building.

ideas.title: Risk and Mobility MGA for home care agencies
ideas.one_liner: Use visit, route and authorization data as the underwriting file for workers' comp, non-owned auto, liability and billing-error cover, and hand agencies the loss-control savings.
ideas.customer: Medicaid agencies with 50-500 aides. First 10: agencies on state-fund or assigned-risk workers' comp in NY, NJ, FL, TX and PA, introduced by two trade associations.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The agency, from the insurance premium line (often the second or third largest cost after wages). Signer: owner or CFO.
ideas.problem: Carriers price home care by payroll class (NCCI 8835 or a state code) and see nothing of the exposure; injuries cluster in patient handling and driving between clients (musculoskeletal 33% of claims in one state study). Brokers earn commission on premium, so loss control that cuts premium cuts their pay; PEOs can't carry Medicaid payment lag.
ideas.solution: An MGA on admitted carrier paper that ingests scheduling and EVV exposure (hours per day, consecutive days, two-person assists, travel legs, vehicle use from phone telematics) with client identity removed; funds lift equipment; manages claims for early return to work; adds recoupment and billing-error cover tied to the Proof-of-Visit evidence pack; bundles payroll and benefits.
ideas.why_now: Immigrant labor losses make injured-aide days costlier; claim scrutiny and recoupment risk are rising; scheduling systems now hold the data.
ideas.wedge: Workers' comp plus billing-error cover for 10 agencies that agree to share de-identified scheduling data.
ideas.path_to_100m: Assume 1.8M agency-employed aides (about 60% of the 2.9M home care workforce, unverified), $28k payroll each, about $50B payroll; workers' comp at about 5% is $2.5B; non-owned auto, liability and billing cover add $1-1.5B, so a $3.5-4B premium pool. The MGA keeps 15-18%, about $525-720M at 100%. $100M needs 14-19% of the pool: heroic. No sourced premium rate for class 8835 was found, so the pool is soft.
ideas.who_does_it_today: PMC Insurance Group (home-health workers' comp program), incumbent carriers and broker programs, state funds, PEOs. Small-business insurtech MGAs exist (Pie, unverified) but none in home care found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Carriers have class codes and no data; brokers are conflicted by commissions; PEOs can't wait 45 days for payment.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a loss-and-exposure data set carriers lack) and switching costs from the bundle.
ideas.earned_secret: Premium follows payroll, but injuries follow visit mix and drive time; the two diverge enough to pick winners. (Unverified.)
ideas.first_90_days: Partner with one carrier; sign a state association; get de-identified data from 10 agencies; price a pilot on paper; file with one state department. Check that using client health data for underwriting is HIPAA-clean.

ideas.title: Continuity Bench: pooled W-2 aides for the TPS and fill-rate gap
ideas.one_liner: A Medicaid-native pool of W-2 aides, work-authorization verified and guaranteed full-time hours, that agencies draw on when staff are lost or hours go unfilled.
ideas.customer: Medicaid agencies that lost workers to TPS and work-permit terminations, and MCOs or states measured on service-start time. First 10: five agencies in Florida, Massachusetts or New Jersey that reported TPS losses, plus one plan paying a fill bounty.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The agency's overtime, recruiting and agency-staffing lines; signer is the administrator or COO. A plan can add a fill-rate incentive from its network-adequacy budget; signer is the VP provider network.
ideas.problem: Medicaid fill rate was 71% for home health aide services (2024 survey), and one LeadingAge member lost 40% of dietary aides and 15% of CNAs overnight when Haiti TPS ended. Each agency is the employer of record, so they can't pool staff, and aides split hours across employers.
ideas.solution: A pooled employer of record with E-Verify, onboarding to each agency's EVV and authorizations, and 32+ guaranteed weekly hours stitched across two or three agencies' routes. Agencies pay wage plus burden plus a spread and still bill Medicaid with the aide as subcontracted staff where the state allows.
ideas.why_now: Supreme Court TPS ruling (Jun 25 2026), Haiti TPS end, about 53,000 TPS holders in health care in 2024; the fill gap predates it.
ideas.wedge: Emergency backfill for TPS-hit agencies at wage plus about $4 an hour.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 1.5B delivered personal-care hours ($46.4B at an assumed $30 an hour) at a 71% fill rate implies about 2.1B authorized and 0.6B unfilled hours. A $3.5-4.5 per hour spread means $100M is 22-29M hours, 4-5% of unfilled hours, about 11,000-14,000 full-time aides; gross billings near $600M. Share needed: about 4-5% of unfilled hours.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ShiftMed/HomeCare.com (W-2, 350K+ worker network including home health and personal care aides, sells to payers and personal care providers) is the biggest risk; Clipboard Health and ShiftKey (contractor model, mostly acute and nursing homes); agencies' own per diem pools.
ideas.why_they_lose: ShiftMed prices as staffing with fixed-rate economics set for higher-wage roles and shows no Medicaid EVV or authorization support on its page. That is a thin edge a staffing firm could close.
ideas.moat: Mainly scale economies in route-stitching density; weak otherwise. Honestly this is a staffing business.
ideas.earned_secret: The binding constraint is fragmented hours, not headcount: an aide with 22 hours across two employers would take 34 if routes and shifts were stitched. (Unverified.)
ideas.first_90_days: Choose a state where staffing firms can supply aides to Medicaid agencies without an extra license; pilot with five agencies; test the plan fill bounty. Check New York's license moratorium and joint-employer rules first.

ideas.title: Partner-not-buy network for independent agencies
ideas.one_liner: Give independent home care agencies the back office, payer contract, insurance and capital of a chain without selling the company.
ideas.customer: Independent owner-operators with $8-15M of Medicaid revenue, many family or immigrant owned, who will not sell. First 10: owners in one state met through trade associations and the HHAX customer base.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The owner, from a management fee out of margin gained; signer is the founder/CEO. MCOs pay through one network contract, with value-based upside shared.
ideas.problem: About 13,000 independent agencies (2021 count) face rate cuts, the TPS loss, EVV enforcement and payer delays while chains buy only those willing to sell. ModivCare's 2025 bankruptcy killed the buy-everything story, and a 2021 attempt at back-office sharing (IHCA, $1.26M pledge) shows no visible traction.
ideas.solution: A management company owning no agencies: shared billing, payroll, EVV compliance, HR and recruiting; group insurance and working capital from the sibling ideas; one delegated-network contract with plans; shared analytics and audit readiness. Owners keep equity and brand. Fee: flat per-claim and per-aide charges for billing and payroll plus a percentage for management services only.
ideas.why_now: Many owners are near exit with few buyers; plans want network adequacy; every 2025-26 shock (rate cuts, TPS, CMS crackdown, NY consolidation, ModivCare) hits small agencies first.
ideas.wedge: Shared compliance and audit readiness plus capital for 10 agencies in one state.
ideas.path_to_100m: A 5% total fee needs $2B of affiliated revenue, about 170-200 agencies at $10-12M, or about 4% of the $46.4B personal-care pool. The 13,000 count is all independent agencies, mostly private-pay; Medicaid-heavy agencies at $10M+ may number 1,500-2,500 (unverified), so it needs 8-12% of those. Share needed: heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Chains that buy (Addus, BrightSpring, Aveanna, Help at Home, Elara, Maxim); agency software (AxisCare, AlayaCare, WellSky, Axxess); IHCA (2021, status unknown); HHAeXchange payer network tools.
ideas.why_they_lose: Chains need control and owners refuse to sell; software vendors sell seats and can't hold payer risk; plans can't sign hundreds of small agencies one at a time.
ideas.moat: Network economies on the payer side (one contract for many agencies) and scale economies in the back office.
ideas.earned_secret: Independent owners will trade a fee for scale and capital but not for equity; whoever offers that first gets the cleanest agencies. (Unverified.)
ideas.first_90_days: Pilot with 10 agencies in one state; build shared billing and a compliance calendar; pre-wire a plan network contract. Legal check first: 42 CFR 447.10(f) bars billing-agent pay that is a percentage of billings or depends on collection (from memory, confirm), so billing fees must be flat or cost-based.

ideas.title: Grease Elevator
ideas.one_liner: Neutral, heated, assayed drop-off terminals where independent grease collectors and small renderers deliver any load size, get paid the same day, and have their oil consolidated into full tankers sold on term contracts with origin paperwork attached: a grain elevator for waste lipids.
ideas.customer: About 3,000 independent used-cooking-oil collectors and small renderers (sellers), and roughly 60 independent biodiesel, renewable-diesel and co-processing buyers that Darling's Diamond Green Diesel does not supply.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Sellers pay handling and storage (about 1-1.5c a lb) and accept index minus a spread; buyers pay a fixed spread over index on 3-12 month contracts. Signers: the collector's owner-operator on the sell side and the producer's VP Feedstock on the buy side. Budget lines: feedstock procurement (buyer), revenue (seller).
ideas.problem: A collector's economics are made or lost between the truck and the plant, not at the restaurant. A route fills 5,000-20,000 lb, a tanker takes 45,000 lb, and he has no heated storage, scale-lab or stop-level paper that EPA auditors (auditing UCO collection locations since July 2023) now expect. The only buyer within 100 miles is the integrated renderer that also competes for his restaurants, so he sells at a posted discount to index, paid in 30+ days (insider claim, unverified). Meanwhile biodiesel plants run at 75-77% utilization against the 90% EPA assumed, and industry groups name feedstock and logistics coordination as the constraint.
ideas.solution: About 40 leased terminal sites (grain elevators, tank farms near rail), each with 200-500k lb of heated tankage, a certified scale, an auto-sampler with rapid assay (FFA, moisture-impurities, phosphorus, chloride), a loading rack and a rail spur where possible. Collectors drop 1,000-45,000 lb, are weighed and sampled, and paid the same day against an electronic warehouse receipt (UCC Article 7) they can pledge for a working-capital advance. GPS/time/photo pickup logs travel with each lot as the origin file. The terminal blends to spec, consolidates into full tankers or rail cars, and sells on term contracts at index plus a fixed spread. It also takes brown grease, DAF fat, small-packer fat and distillers corn oil from independent ethanol plants.
ideas.why_now: OPIS projects biomass-based diesel feedstock demand of 34.2B lb (2025), 53.8B (2026) and 62.0B (2027); independents are restarting and running at 75-77%; UCO imports fell 38% (China-origin down 67%); D4 RINs at 210-236c mean the paper on a load is worth about as much as the oil; EPA UCO audits and the 2028 import-RIN reduction make origin files valuable.
ideas.wedge: Three terminals in Iowa/Minnesota/Illinois (soy-biodiesel restarts plus rail to the Gulf) and one in the Southeast. First ten customers: eight independent collectors within 100 miles of each site and two independent producers (the kind of buyer restarting now, such as Minnesota Soybean Processors' Brewster plant or FutureFuel's Batesville plant).
ideas.path_to_100m: 40 terminals x 50M lb = 2.0B lb a year x 5c all-in (1.5c handling + 2.5c merchandising spread + 1c blend/finance) = $100M net margin on about $1.3B gross sales. 2.0B lb is 3.7% of 2026 feedstock demand (OPIS) and about 30% of a 6-7B lb 'small-supplier' universe (my estimate: ~1.8B lb independent UCO from EIA yellow-grease run rate of 7.3B lb less ~3.3B lb imports, Darling and RTI; ~2B lb small-renderer/packer fat; ~2B lb DCO from independent ethanol plants; ~0.5B lb brown grease). Capex $1-3M a site if leased ($40-120M) plus ~$40M working capital. Heroic share; the 5c is an insider guess.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Darling/Valley transfer stations (captive); Baker Commodities, Sanimax, Griffin and other independent renderers; brokers (Targray, ISCC-certified); Tagaddod (MENA aggregation, $26.3M Series A); Neste's Mahoney Environmental; RTI's closed loop; tank terminals (Vopak, Kinder Morgan) that do not take small drops or assay them. No neutral multi-site drop-off network found (not exhaustively searched).
ideas.why_they_lose: Darling cannot be neutral: it competes with every collector for restaurant contracts and with every independent producer for supply, and sells to DGD first (DGD was about 20% of Darling's net sales in H1 2026, secondary source). Global traders need 5,000-tonne lots. Terminals do not do assays, stop-level paper or same-day pay on 3,000-lb drops.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (terminal density shortens hauls; lab and scale cost spread over volume) plus counter-positioning against integrated renderers, switching costs (receipts, advances, paper) and a transaction-price dataset. The digest's marketplace-owned logistics, payments and credit flywheel.
ideas.earned_secret: Collectors do not lose money finding restaurants; they lose it on the last 100 miles and the 30-day pay. The small-lot discount, the slow pay and the missing paper are one problem because nobody neutral sits between truck and plant. (Insider claim; verify against 30 settlement sheets.)
ideas.first_90_days: Collect 20 collector settlement sheets and match them to the index to measure the real discount; interview 8 buyer feedstock heads; lease one site and price tankage and scale; pre-sell a 6-month term to one producer; settle the electronic warehouse-receipt structure and line up a lender for advances.

ideas.title: Bankable Supply
ideas.one_liner: A pooled-supply company that signs 3-7 year feedstock supply agreements (volume bands, index plus fixed fee, a carbon-intensity true-up, a delivery guarantee) with independent renewable-diesel, biodiesel, SAF and co-processing projects, and fills them back-to-back from hundreds of small collectors, renderers, ethanol plants and crushers.
ideas.customer: Independent producers and developers that cannot get a long-term contract today: restarting biodiesel plants, farmer-owned renewable-diesel and SAF projects, refinery co-processors. About 30-40 projects (my estimate).
ideas.payer_and_signer: CFO or project-finance lead plus VP Feedstock at the producer; the lender's technical advisor must bless the terms. Budget: feedstock cost, plus a financing condition that currently has no owner.
ideas.problem: Project lenders need a 5-10 year feedstock agreement with a creditworthy counterparty. Independents get either a parent that supplies everything (XCF's New Rise Reno buys all non-food feedstock from Phillips 66 at spot plus fees, a single-counterparty risk its 10-K flags) or a trader (Trafigura supplies about 470,000 t a year of UCO to Brazil's Acelen behind a $1.5B financing). In the US the independent middle has neither: Darling will not supply competitors of DGD, crushers sell soybean oil on annual terms, and 3,000 collectors cannot sign ten-year take-or-pay. In January 2026 producers were reported to be hesitating on long-term deals because 2026-27 CI scores were unsettled.
ideas.solution: Sign supply agreements on a standard form with a CI true-up clause (price adjusts to the final 45Z emissions rate), volume bands and a replacement-supply guarantee backed by reinsurance. Fill them from 300+ supplier contracts, Grease Elevator terminals and ethanol-plant corn oil; hedge flat price back-to-back; carry origin files on every lot.
ideas.why_now: 2027 demand is 81% above 2025 (OPIS); 45Z final rules due November 2026; EPA's reallocation proposal due by end of October; the 2028 import-RIN reduction turns domestic-origin certainty into the product; plants are restarting. The pending rules are exactly why nobody is signing, so the first standard form wins.
ideas.wedge: One 3-year, 250M lb a year agreement with an independent producer, filled from four Grease Elevator terminals, two ethanol-plant corn-oil contracts and one mid-size renderer. First ten suppliers signed on letters of intent before the producer signs.
ideas.path_to_100m: 20 agreements x 250M lb = 5.0B lb x 2c net (0.8c logistics, 0.7c risk and guarantee, 0.5c CI/true-up) = $100M net on about $3.2B gross sales, 9% of 2026 feedstock volume (OPIS). Capital: ~$150M working capital, hedging lines and a reinsurance layer from infrastructure or credit funds. Moderately heroic; counterparty concentration (two or three buyers could be 60% of volume) is the main risk.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Darling (captive to DGD), Chevron REG and Phillips 66 (captive), trader-backed supply abroad (Trafigura/Acelen), Targray (ISCC-certified trading), Tagaddod (MENA aggregation), crushers (annual soybean oil contracts). No US independent pooled-supply aggregator found (not exhaustively searched).
ideas.why_they_lose: Darling is conflicted; traders prefer 5,000-tonne lots and will not carry first-mile risk; crushers sell one feedstock; lenders will not accept spot.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (portfolio of supplier contracts and terminals), scale economies in procurement, switching costs (agreements pledged under project debt) and counter-positioning against integrated renderers.
ideas.earned_secret: A lender does not care that the oil is 3c cheaper; it cares that someone creditworthy owes delivery for ten years. A feedstock buyer spends half his year proving that (supplier audits, backup suppliers, force-majeure language) and still cannot sign small suppliers. The same pooled paper solves both.
ideas.first_90_days: Get term sheets from two independent producers; interview 10 project-finance technical advisors for the exact terms they require; sign letters of intent with 10 suppliers; line up a hedging counterparty and one reinsurer for the delivery guarantee; draft the CI true-up clause with a 45Z tax lawyer once the November rule lands.

ideas.title: Cleared Lot
ideas.one_liner: The PSA of waste lipids: a private grade and sealed-sample certificate for every load of UCO, tallow and corn oil with a binding deduction schedule so gate-lab disputes disappear, an origin file, and an RIN/45Z eligibility warranty sold through an independent insurer.
ideas.customer: Producers and refiners that buy waste-derived and imported lipids (buyers); collectors and aggregators (sellers).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Sellers pay $60-90 a lot for sealed sampling, assay and the certificate; buyers pay a warranty premium of about 0.3-0.6c a lb on high-risk lots. Signers: VP Feedstock, Head of Compliance (RIN) and CFO (45Z).
ideas.problem: On my arithmetic one 45,000-lb UCO load carries about $32k of credit-stack value (about $21.9k RIN at $2.20 and 1.7 RINs a gallon, ~$2.9k 45Z, ~$7k LCFS) against about $24.8k of oil. Obligated parties that retire invalid RINs must replace them unless they hold verified RINs (my reading of the RFS quality-assurance rules; confirm with counsel). EPA has audited UCO supply chains since 2023, senators called its verification meaningless in 2024 letters, and 45Z insurance excludes fraud, known risks and change in law. At the gate, buyers and sellers argue over free fatty acids, impurities and metals every week.
ideas.solution: (1) Tamper-evident auto-sampler at the loading rack, rapid assay (FFA, moisture-impurities, XRF metals) and a risk-based isotope/fatty-acid fingerprint on a sample of lots. (2) A one-page lot certificate that contracts reference: it fixes the deduction schedule and attaches stop-level origin logs and weigh tickets. (3) A lot-level eligibility warranty written by a separate insurer/MGA so the verifier stays independent. (4) Payment instruction and a transaction-based price index as by-products.
ideas.why_now: D4 RIN above $2; 45Z credits first being sold (80-93c on the dollar); import-RIN haircut from 2028 makes origin a per-lot fact; 62B lb of feedstock by 2027; EPA audits.
ideas.wedge: Sell side: the same 20 collectors using Grease Elevator terminals. Buy side: three independent producers that restarted and have thin compliance teams. Start with imported and mixed-origin UCO lots, which carry the most disallowance risk.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 25B lb a year of waste-derived lipids (EIA July run rate: UCO 7.3B lb, tallow 9.3B, corn oil 5.4B, other greases ~3B). About 450k lots x $75 = $34M of assay fees, plus warranty on 15B lb x 0.5c = $75M, total ~$110M. That needs a majority of waste-derived lots, so the standard must win; at 25% share it is ~$28M. Heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: SGS, Intertek, Bureau Veritas/Inspectorate, Saybolt, AmSpec, Alfred H Knight (inspection); EcoEngineers (an LRQA company) and other EPA-approved QAP providers; Veriflux and Verity/CIBO (software); Marsh and IMA (45Z tax-credit insurance); ISCC (a sustainability scheme, not a lot-level assay).
ideas.why_they_lose: Inspectors sell hours and are paid by traders; QAP auditors sample after the fact and cannot also be the insurer; software providers cannot touch the oil; none can bind buyer and seller to one deduction schedule. Darling's paper is private to Darling.
ideas.moat: Network standard (contracts cite the grade), capacity-limited lab network (the PSA analogue), loss data for underwriting. Race-the-bundle risk: Darling or a large inspector could ship a certificate, so a second product (warranty or index) must exist first.
ideas.earned_secret: At a refinery the lab at the gate is the real contract. Buyers pay a fear premium for suppliers they trust because untrusted lots cost rejected loads, catalyst life and compliance risk; a trustworthy sealed sample is worth more than 1c a lb even when the oil is identical. (Insider claim; verify in 90 days.)
ideas.first_90_days: Get 12 months of reject and dispute history from three buyers; pilot sealed samplers at two terminals; interview two 45Z insurers and one QAP provider on independence and exclusions; confirm with RFS counsel who bears replacement liability; price-test $60 / $90 / $120 a lot.

ideas.title: Oil Yield Partner
ideas.one_liner: Zero-capex, pay-from-the-oil upgrades of corn-oil recovery at ethanol plants: we install and run the extraction system, guarantee the yield, and take a share of the extra oil for five years, after which the plant owns the equipment.
ideas.customer: The 189 US ethanol plants (EIA, 1 Jan 2026), mostly farmer-owned LLCs with risk-averse boards.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Plant general manager and board; no capex line, paid out of incremental oil revenue.
ideas.problem: Average US plants recover 0.75-0.90 lb of corn oil a bushel against a theoretical 1.9 and a practical ceiling near 1.3 (Novozymes, IFF). Elite Octane reports 1.31 lb a bushel after ICM's FOT; IFF reports 0.89 to 1.03 from enzymes alone. On a 29M-bushel plant the gap is about 10M lb a year, about $7M at 70c. Only about 8 plants had installed or were building FOT by Oct 2024.
ideas.solution: Choose and install the best of Fluid Quip, Valicor, ICM and enzyme systems per plant, operate with remote process control, guarantee yield (pay the shortfall), market the oil in pooled lots with origin and CI files, and take 30-35% of the incremental oil for five years.
ideas.why_now: The deep-pocketed buyer is renewable diesel (62B lb by 2027) and the new supply it needs without land, cattle or imports is oil already inside the corn: ~2B lb extra is ~4% of 2026 demand (my arithmetic, 5.5B bushels x 0.35 lb). Oil at ~70c turned a multi-year payback into under one year.
ideas.wedge: Ten plants in one rail-served corridor with a Fluid Quip or Valicor install base, a guaranteed floor and a pooled oil lot sold to one producer. First customers: plants that have not committed to FOT and whose lender covenants allow a revenue share.
ideas.path_to_100m: 40 plants x 10.2M lb extra a year x 70c x 35% share = about $100M, i.e. 21% of plants, with ~$240M capex ($6M a plant). Honest check: a plant that can self-fund pays back in ~0.85 year, so only plants that will not self-fund (perhaps 40%) are addressable, making this over half of the addressable set. Heroic; the window is probably 18-24 months, and lender consent (CoBank, AgStar and others often restrict liens and revenue sharing) is a gate.
ideas.who_does_it_today: ICM (FOT, ~8 sites), Fluid Quip Technologies (DCO systems), Valicor ($4.4M modular unit), Novonesis and IFF (enzymes), plant in-house teams. No revenue-share or yield-guarantee provider found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Vendors sell equipment once and are not paid for yield; they will not guarantee the oil, and their incentive is the sale.
ideas.moat: Process power from a cross-plant yield dataset and switching costs from the guarantee; weak, because OEMs can add a finance arm.
ideas.earned_secret: A plant manager's problem is not the payback; it is who gets blamed if the new skid misses its number. A yield guarantee moves that risk off his board.
ideas.first_90_days: Pull yield data from 15 plants; get a vendor price on a modular system; ask two lenders whether a revenue share is permitted; price the guarantee; sign one pilot with no capex.

ideas.title: Second Stream
ideas.one_liner: Put an automatic grease-removal unit at fryer-heavy restaurants and collect the skimmed grease on the same stop as the used cooking oil: the restaurant pays a flat fee that is less than it saves on pump-outs, and we sell the grease as feedstock.
ideas.customer: About 700,000 US restaurants have grease traps or interceptors (my estimate). Target fryer-heavy, high-volume sites (quick service, chicken, burger, hotels, casinos) pumped monthly to quarterly.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Restaurant owner or GM (budget line: grease-trap maintenance, about $350-500 a pump-out, 4-12 a year, plus fines of $200-5,000 an incident); chains: facilities director. City FOG inspectors are the push.
ideas.problem: EPA estimates 800-17,000 lb a year of fats, oils and grease per restaurant. An automatic removal unit typically takes 7-10 lb a day at a high-volume burger restaurant (2,500-3,650 lb a year), fresh and mostly water-free. Haulers pump the trap, dewater it and landfill or treat it, so most of this fat is wasted as feedstock while the restaurant pays for the pumping.
ideas.solution: Place units (leased, financed), install, and bundle a flat monthly service with a weekly skimmed-grease pickup on the existing used-oil route. Sell the grease as brown-grade feedstock with origin logs. Pump-outs drop to one or two a year for solids.
ideas.why_now: Waste-lipid prices are at records, North American-origin waste is the 45Z-favoured feed, and brown grease is the least-contested pool of domestic fat. Greasezilla and bp have shown a buyer will fund recovery, but only at the treatment plant.
ideas.wedge: One metro with an active FOG ordinance that accepts certified units: 150 quick-service and hotel kitchens signed through a UCO collector partner, with pump-out logs as the baseline for a savings guarantee.
ideas.path_to_100m: 46,000 sites x $2,250 a year = ~$103M ($1,200 service fee + ~3,000 lb of skimmed grease at 35c, my estimate) is ~6.6% of the interceptor base. Gross margin ~$650 a site (~29%) after hardware amortization and marginal route cost; capex ~$230M ($5k a site). Check: DAR PRO already visits ~200,000 locations and LES-style haulers hold the pump-out revenue.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Liquid Environmental Solutions (Goldman Sachs Alternatives; trap pumping, treatment plants and UCO), Denali (TPG), DAR PRO (Darling); Greasezilla (at the treatment plant, 24 sites, bp-financed expansion); unit makers Thermaco/Big Dipper, Highland Tank and others (hardware, not routes). No source-capture service paying restaurants found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Haulers are paid per pump-out and own treatment plants that charge tipping fees; a unit that cuts pumping cuts their revenue. Unit makers sell through plumbing distributors and do not run routes.
ideas.moat: Route density plus switching costs (installed hardware and multi-year service contract) and counter-positioning against pumpers.
ideas.earned_secret: A UCO driver is already at the back door every week; the second stream costs a minute of stop time and is the restaurant's biggest hidden bill. Everyone who sells the unit leaves out the pickup; everyone who owns the pickup sells pump-outs.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 fast-food and hotel GMs on pump-out invoices; confirm the unit is accepted as an interceptor in three metros (ASME A112.14.3 or PDI-G101 certification); get a unit-maker price; find a UCO collector to co-run; test the 35c grease price with two buyers.

ideas.title: Oil Check
ideas.one_liner: Pay soybean farmers for the oil they deliver: per-load oil, protein and moisture settlement at independent elevators and farmer-owned crushers, a variety-level pounds-of-oil-per-acre score for seed choice, and identity-preserved premium contracts funded by the crusher's extra margin.
ideas.customer: Farmer-owned and independent crushers and their elevators; farmers (indirectly); seed companies for variety data.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Crusher's head of origination or CEO (cooperatives: GM and board). Budget line: grain-origination premiums, paid as a share of the extra margin.
ideas.problem: Oil is about 50% of crush value (CME oilshare 50.65% in March 2026 against a long-run ~37%), yet beans are still bought by the bushel at one price. The crusher measures oil and protein at the gate and keeps the variation. A Purdue/Iowa State estimate put the gain from sorting at 12c a bushel on average and 25c at most (older data); one processor already pays elevators on protein and oil via an estimated processing value, but not nationally. NOPA oil yield runs 11.3-11.8 lb a bushel; one point of oil is ~0.5 lb a bushel, ~$0.35 at 70c, less ~$0.10-0.15 of meal lost to the oil-protein trade-off (my arithmetic).
ideas.solution: Per-load NIR oil and moisture at the pit, a settlement engine paying a premium on processing value, variety scores from yield times oil, and contracts telling farmers which varieties to plant. Priced as a share of the crusher's extra margin.
ideas.why_now: The oil share flipped in 2025-26, meal is at its lowest since 2016 (DTN), biofuel use is 54% of soybean oil, and oil per acre is now the right target. Moisture is a further lever.
ideas.wedge: Two farmer-owned processors and 30 elevators in one state, 200,000 acres, one crop year of data, and a premium paid on the top quartile.
ideas.path_to_100m: Program fee 4c a bushel x 1.5B bushels (60% of a ~2.5B bushel crush, my estimate) = $60M; settlement software 0.5c x 2.5B = $12.5M; variety data and seed licensing $10M; adding corn for ethanol (oil and starch) at 1.5c x 1.0B bushels = $15M. Total ~$97M, which needs well over half of US crush: heroic, and the big three crushers profit from the status quo.
ideas.who_does_it_today: One processor's protein-and-oil premium program (source did not name it); seed companies (Corteva, Bayer and others) market yield, not oil per acre; grain software such as Bushel settles by grade. Nobody found doing national composition-priced settlement.
ideas.why_they_lose: ADM, Bunge and Cargill earn extra margin from receiving high-oil beans at a flat price, so paying for oil gives it away; elevators bear the cost of measuring and capture none of the gain.
ideas.moat: Variety-level oil-per-acre data plus a payment rail; switching costs once farmers plant by it; counter-positioning against the large crushers.
ideas.earned_secret: Dairy moved from volume to components pricing decades ago; soybeans have not because the party that sees the composition (the crusher) is also the party that benefits from hiding it.
ideas.first_90_days: Pull gate NIR data from two farmer-owned crushers; build the oil-per-acre score from public variety trials; interview 15 elevator managers; price a premium schedule that leaves the crusher 60% of the gain.

ideas.title: Co-Pro Desk
ideas.one_liner: Sell petroleum refiners hydrotreater-ready lipid feed, receiving skids, 14C sampling and RIN accounting as one service on a RIN-linked formula, so they can generate their own D4 RINs instead of buying them at $2.20.
ideas.customer: About 120 US refineries with distillate hydrotreaters, starting with obligated merchant refiners that are RIN-short; not the integrated renewable-diesel majors.
ideas.payer_and_signer: VP Supply and Trading or the refinery manager; budget line: RIN purchases, the obligated party's largest compliance cost.
ideas.problem: EPA set record obligations (25.82B RINs in 2026), D4 RINs rose from 163c in February to 210-236c in August and moved between ~191c and 236c in the last week of August as exemption decisions landed (1.76B RINs exempted for 29 small refineries on 31 August). Topsoe says up to 10% renewable feed can go into a diesel hydrotreater with limited modifications, and bp's Cherry Point refinery reports more than 7,000 barrels a day of co-processing capability, yet few refiners have receiving tanks, a feed spec or a way to measure the renewable fraction.
ideas.solution: Pre-treated lipids (low phosphorus and metals) in tank trucks or rail cars; heated receiving skid; catalyst and unit support through the licensors; ASTM D6866 carbon-14 testing per batch; EMTS/RIN reporting; formula pricing tied to RIN and diesel.
ideas.why_now: RINs up ~45% this year, RVO up ~60%, producers under-running at 75-78%, import supply falling. Refiners are the one buyer class that is short the credit.
ideas.wedge: Three merchant refiners with a diesel hydrotreater and rail access, a 3-5% co-processing trial and a single-lot guarantee on feed spec.
ideas.path_to_100m: 25 refineries x 150M lb a year = 3.75B lb x 2.5c net = ~$94M on ~$2.4B gross (7% of 2026 demand). Per refinery, 150M lb is ~19.5M gallons: ~33M RINs ($73M at $2.20) plus $49M of displaced diesel against ~$98M of feed and ~$10M processing, roughly $14M a year before 45Z or LCFS (my arithmetic). Thin, but self-generated RINs cost ~$1.76 each against $2.20 bought. Legal premises to confirm: EPA's carbon-14 approach for co-processed fuel, 45Z treatment of co-processed fuel (unverified), unit constraints.
ideas.who_does_it_today: bp Cherry Point and a few others (not verified); licensors Topsoe, Honeywell UOP, Axens (technology); catalyst makers; 14C labs such as Beta Analytic; DGD and full-conversion plants (not co-processing). Nobody found selling feed, skids, testing and RIN accounting as a package.
ideas.why_they_lose: Licensors sell technology, not molecules; Darling will not supply refiners that compete with DGD; traders cannot pre-treat; labs only test.
ideas.moat: Process power (feed spec learned unit by unit), switching costs (the unit is tuned to our feed) and data.
ideas.earned_secret: A refinery does not need a renewable-diesel plant to make RINs; it needs a 3-5% blend its operators trust. The blocker is a feed they can specify, a tank they can heat and a lab number they can defend, not RIN economics.
ideas.first_90_days: Interview 20 refinery supply managers and 5 hydrotreater licensors; get EPA counsel's read on 14C co-processing registration and 45Z treatment; price a 3% pilot on a 40 kb/d unit; line up pre-treated feed from one terminal.

ideas.title: Premium Ledger
ideas.one_liner: Measure each lot's carbon intensity from plant-level actuals (rendering and crush-plant energy, transport mode, allocation, farm practices) and clear the premium between supplier and producer by formula, taking a fee on the premium and a share of the credit that default scores leave unclaimed.
ideas.customer: About 90 US biomass-based diesel producers and their roughly 1,500 first-tier suppliers (renderers, crushers, UCO aggregators, ethanol corn-oil plants).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Producer's CFO or VP Tax, and VP Feedstock. Budget line: the CI premium they already pay (about $970M a year, my arithmetic) and the credit they are not claiming.
ideas.problem: Under 45Z a gallon earns up to $1.00 x (50 - CI)/50 when wage rules are met (my reading of the statute), so each CI point is worth ~$0.02 a gallon. Most producers file with GREET defaults because measured numbers need data from five to eight parties. USDA's FD-CIC final rule (effective 29 July) and the June GREET update reward measured inputs but give no rail to collect and verify them; 45Z credits trade at 5-11% discounts partly because buyers need diligence.
ideas.solution: A supplier-data network with meter and bill ingestion, mass-balance across the chain, and lot-level CI packages for the producer's independent verifier (the platform does not verify). Premium paid by formula: dollars a lb = f(measured CI points, current credit value per point), settled through the same ledger as Cleared Lot.
ideas.why_now: FD-CIC effective 29 July 2026; final 45Z rules due November 2026; first returns in 2027; credit buyers diligence at a discount.
ideas.wedge: UCO, tallow and corn-oil chains (three hops, ten buyers), then soy crush plants.
ideas.path_to_100m: Premium flows ~$970M a year (UCO 7.3B lb x 5.1c, tallow 9.3B x 3.7c, corn oil 5.4B x 4.7c) x 8% clearing fee = $78M, plus 20% of unlocked uplift (3 CI points x $0.02 x ~3B waste-based gallons = $180M, so $36M) = ~$114M, but only at near-total share of the waste-lipid chain. Adding soybean/canola farm-level CI (5-8 points on ~2.2B gallons = $220-350M of uplift) or corn for ethanol (5.8c a bushel per CI point, trade-article figure) is what makes the share plausible. Heroic; closest to dead.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Veriflux (1B lb traced since 2020; EPA/45Z/LCFS records, 850 companies), Verity/Gevo with CIBO (field-level data), EcoEngineers and other consultants/verifiers, Truterra, Indigo, Bushel, Regrow and crushers' own programs on the farm side.
ideas.why_they_lose: Software firms do not touch the oil and cannot bind a price formula; consultants bill hours; crushers will not give suppliers a share of credit they keep.
ideas.moat: A supplier-data network and a formula that becomes the contract reference; weak, and it should be treated as a feature of Cleared Lot unless a producer pays for it alone.
ideas.earned_secret: Auditors know where the points hide: transport miles and mode, steam fuel at rendering plants, co-product allocation and farm practices. Most are reachable only if someone collects primary data from a plant manager who has no reason to answer a producer's email.
ideas.first_90_days: Pull default and actual CI inputs for 10 UCO and tallow lots; measure the average gap; ask three producers what they would pay per CI point; stop if the gap is under 2 points.

ideas.title: Siap Masak: certified cook-ready prep plants for 4-hour kitchens
ideas.one_liner: Move the riskiest, most labour-heavy step (raw chicken and vegetable handling) out of 27,820 volunteer-run kitchens into audited plants that deliver portion-weighed, chilled, cook-ready kits timed to the new 4-hour rule.
ideas.customer: Kepala SPPG and mitra/yayasan of full-size kitchens (2,000-3,000 portions) within about a 2-hour chilled-delivery radius of a plant; start in dense Java and Sumatra clusters (Bogor-Bekasi-Karawang, Sidoarjo-Mojokerto, Medan-Deli Serdang).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The kitchen's ingredient line (Rp10k per portion, about $300-410k a year per kitchen) paid from its BGN virtual account, which needs two approvals: the yayasan/mitra representative and the Kepala SPPG. Cluster deals are signed by the chair of a mitra group (Kadin, Muhammadiyah or NU unit) with a written no-objection from the BGN regional coordinator.
ideas.problem: The August rules squeeze a 3,000-portion cook into a three-hour night window (cook from about 02:00, eat within 4 hours; Kepala SPPG must be on site 02:00-08:00). Volunteers wash, cut and portion about 350 chickens and 350 kg of vegetables per cook day in that window, which is where cross-contamination and time-temperature errors happen. BGN's own analysis of 70 incidents points at Salmonella on chicken, eggs and vegetables and E. coli on water, rice, tofu and chicken, not chemical poison. BGN's response is test kits for arsenic and spoilage (only 'considered' on 17-18 Aug) plus closures (504 permanent, 1,999 closed 7 Sep).
ideas.solution: NKV-registered (poultry), halal-certified, HACCP plants (leased first) deliver uncooked-but-prepared kits: portion-cut and weighed chicken, washed and cut vegetables, graded and sanitised eggs, in coded trays arriving 00:00-01:30 by our reefer vans. Each batch has a QR with farm, plant, temperature and weight data. Kitchens still cook, so the 4-hour rule is untouched. Price stays inside the Rp10k cap by capturing the farm-to-wet-market spread; plants buy from local farmer cooperatives so sellers of record stay eligible under Peraturan BGN 10/2026.
ideas.why_now: 4-hour rule and consumption label (6-11 Aug 2026); Kepala SPPG on-site rule (26 Aug); SLHS deadline 10 Aug and the closure wave; Peraturan BGN 10/2026 (in force 18 Aug) names certified processors as eligible suppliers; Berastagi and Jayapura poisonings cost kitchen heads their jobs.
ideas.wedge: One leased NKV poultry cut-up room plus cold store serving 25-40 kitchens in one regency with chicken and vegetable kits only (the two biggest handling items in BGN's per-cook numbers). First 10 customers: kitchens that were suspended or classed 'critical' (654), plus the kitchens of one mitra group.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Chicken plus vegetables per full-size kitchen is about $136k a year (420 kg chicken on 88 days at Rp40k/kg = $92k; 350 kg vegetables on 220 days at Rp9k/kg = $43k). Cross-check: 27,820 kitchens x $92k = $2.6B, matching Bisnis's 1.1 Mt-of-chicken headline at Rp38k/kg. A plant serving 100 kitchens is about $13.6M of revenue, so $100M of revenue is about 7.4 plants and 740 kitchens: 2.7% of kitchens and about 2.4% of the $5.6B chicken-plus-vegetable flow. Gross margin 12-15% means about $13-15M gross profit at $100M revenue; capex about $4-6M per leased-and-fitted plant. $100M of gross profit would need roughly 20% of kitchens.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Japfa (15 poultry slaughterhouses, 78 breeding farms, national cold storage; says it supplies some kitchens), Charoen Pokphand (processed chicken about 15% of H1 2026 sales), Malindo; wet-market slaughterhouses and traders; Eden Farm and Sayurbox (Jabodetabek B2B fresh, no MBG role found); Chickin (said it hopes to join MBG); each kitchen in-house with volunteers; Polri's own warehouses and farms for its kitchens. No supplier of cook-ready kits timed to SPPG schedules found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Integrators sell standard SKUs through distributors, are not the micro/small/cooperative sellers the rules favour, and run no per-kitchen night-delivery windows. B2B startups have no plants and focus on Jabodetabek. Traders have no cold chain, NKV or paperwork. Kitchens cannot fix handling with volunteers on a 3-hour clock.
ideas.moat: Process power (HACCP and time-temperature discipline the kitchen cannot replicate) plus cornered resource (certified capacity near clusters and farmer-cooperative offtake); scale economies in routes at 30+ kitchens per plant.
ideas.earned_secret: In outbreak investigations the culprit is almost never poison; it is time, temperature and raw handling. Test kits catch arsenic and spoilage, not Salmonella, B. cereus or E. coli, and a kitchen is inspected once for its SLHS while a plant can be audited daily. The new 4-hour rule makes it worse: more raw handling by tired volunteers in less time. Move the raw step upstream into a place you can inspect every day.
ideas.first_90_days: Recruit a retired Dinkes/BPOM food-safety lead and a HACCP auditor; lease one NKV poultry room and cold store near a dense cluster; run chicken and vegetable kits for five kitchens logging time and temperature and counting incidents; get written confirmation from BGN's food-safety deputy and a regional coordinator that certified uncooked inputs are acceptable under Keputusan 401.1/2025 and the 4-hour rule (legal premise, unverified: no ban found but no primary text read); sign a supply MoU with one poultry farmer cooperative.

ideas.title: Satu Faktur: kecamatan consolidation hubs in idle Kopdes cold stores
ideas.one_liner: Run the state-built Kopdes cold-store warehouse in each kecamatan as the one place that turns 15-40 eligible micro-suppliers into one purchase order, one invoice, one delivery and one payment per kitchen, with the cooperative as the legal seller of record.
ideas.customer: The 27,820 kitchens (about 3.9 per kecamatan on roughly 7,200 kecamatan) and the Kopdes Merah Putih boards that own an empty warehouse with cold storage, a logistics vehicle and a Rp3B Himbara loan.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Kitchens pay through the VA (the service fee is carved from the same Rp10k, not added); signers are the Kepala SPPG plus the yayasan representative. The Kopdes board chair signs the management contract; the Himbara regional commercial/micro head sponsors it (protecting a Rp3B loan); at scale the Kemenkop deputy minister for cooperatives.
ideas.problem: Rules now require at least 15 eligible suppliers per kitchen (widely reported), local-first sourcing, NIB and NPWP, tax withholding, BGN-format budget lines, no mark-ups and no commissions, on pain of suspension or dismissal; on 29 Sep the Attorney General named the former BGN leadership as suspects. The Kepala SPPG's problem is paperwork and personal liability, not price. Meanwhile 14,442 Kopdes buildings with a mandated cold store and vehicle are complete (most idle: only 1,061 inaugurated as operating in May), and Kopdes loan instalments fell due 25 Sep.
ideas.solution: A hub operated under a management contract inside the Kopdes warehouse: receive from local farmers, millers and processors; weigh, grade, temperature-check and document; consolidate per kitchen per day; issue one e-faktur invoice; print BGN-format budget lines; pay suppliers within 48 hours (funded by an early-pay discount); keep price-benchmark logs that make a mark-up impossible and a dispute short. The cooperative is the seller of record so Peraturan BGN 10/2026 eligibility holds. The hub is also the physical node for the BGN portal's seven mandated commodities.
ideas.why_now: Peraturan BGN 10/2026 (18 Aug); SE 14/2026 pushing poultry through farmer cooperatives (12 Aug); portal announcement 12 and 17 Sep with marketplace partners wanted; Kopdes instalments due 25 Sep; Kejagung (29 Sep) makes defensible buying worth more than cheap buying.
ideas.wedge: Three districts with a finished gerai, a working cold room and four or more kitchens; run eggs, chicken and vegetables first. First 10 customers: Kepala SPPG in those kecamatan; first sponsor: the Himbara branch holding the Kopdes loan.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Average hub gross merchandise value is 3.9 kitchens x about $300k = $1.16M a year. At a 6% consolidation fee that is $69k of revenue per hub, so $100M needs about 1,440 hubs (20% of kecamatan and 20% of the $8.3B ingredient flow). Adding supplier early-pay discount and documentation fees (8.5% take) gives $98k per hub and about 1,020 hubs (14%). If the cooperative books sales and we earn management fee plus margin, $100M of principal sales is about 85 hubs but net take is only 6-8%. Share needed is 14-20%: heroic, made less hopeless only because the portal mandate for seven commodities, not persuasion of each kitchen, supplies the volume.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Telkom Digi Koperasi (software for 80,081 coops) and BRILink; Agrinas Pangan with TNI (builds the gerai); ID FOOD (dry goods to 108 coops); Bulog (rice); the BGN portal itself (SIPLah model, 15 SIPLah marketplace operators including Telkom/Xooply); Sayurbox, Eden Farm, Chickin; farmer associations' direct-sale deals (East Java eggs); informal tengkulak; Pintek-style supplier finance on SIPLah (2021). No operator running Kopdes warehouses as MBG hubs found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Telkom sells software to bookkeepers, not field operations; Himbara cannot operate what it lends to; marketplaces cannot hold cold chain; integrators are not eligible sellers and conflict with their own distributors; tengkulak cannot produce NIB, NPWP and e-faktur without exposing margin; Kopdes boards were appointed in a rush and have six business lines to run.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (management contracts in each kecamatan where the cooperative is the eligible seller, plus Himbara sponsorship) and switching costs (a kitchen's budget-line history, supplier network and payment record live in the hub).
ideas.earned_secret: A Kepala SPPG will pay for the most defensible purchase, not the cheapest: after the Attorney General's announcement nobody wants to sign an invoice they cannot explain. A coop manager knows village cooperatives only survive with a guaranteed anchor buyer (old KUDs lived on sugar mills and milk processors), MBG is the only anchor on offer, and the Rp3B loan clock is the lever.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign management MoUs with three Kopdes boards and their Himbara branches; recruit a Kopdes veteran and an ex-BGN accountant; start egg, chicken and vegetable lanes for six kitchens; produce BGN-format lines and pay suppliers T+2; measure rejected lines before and after. Check the legal premise (unverified): that a private operator may run a Kopdes warehouse with the coop as seller of record under Peraturan BGN 10/2026 and the portal terms, and that the hub fee is an allowable at-cost line, not a commission.

ideas.title: Franchisor-in-a-box for the institutional operator groups
ideas.one_liner: Sell the HQ functions a franchisor would have (central lab, procurement master agreement, lender reporting, training) to the handful of institutional groups that run hundreds of kitchens under one chain of command.
ideas.customer: Yayasan Kemala Bhayangkari/Polri (1,179 kitchens in Feb 2026; 1,415 built and 828 operating by June; target 1,500), Kadin (742nd kitchen opened 6 Mar 2026; target 1,000), TNI (2,000 targeted), BIN (1,000), NU (1,000), Muhammadiyah (500); the last four are March 2025 targets, unverified.
ideas.payer_and_signer: HQ operations/logistics heads under a master services agreement, paid per kitchen per month from the at-cost operating line and the facility incentive: for Polri the Kapolri's logistics assistant and the chair of Yayasan Kemala Bhayangkari; for Kadin its chair and MBG task-force head.
ideas.problem: BGN capped each yayasan at 10 kitchens (Polri reportedly exempt per ICW), so about 13,000 mitra are too small to buy anything; the only owners with command-and-control are institutions, which are franchisors without a franchise toolkit. Polri builds warehouses (18, rising to 28 of 1,000 t), farms and a feed mill, yet purchases are still kitchen by kitchen from selected suppliers; their kitchens carry Himbara and cooperative loans needing covenant-grade reporting; ICW has asked the KPK to oversee them.
ideas.solution: (1) A central accredited lab and retention-sample programme; (2) master supply agreements with Kopdes and farmer cooperatives for the seven commodities, executed through hubs and plants; (3) lender reporting from VA data, compliance (SLHS, IPAL, BPJS) and incident dashboards; (4) a training academy for the 47-person crews. Pricing about $1k per kitchen-month plus a 2.5% procurement margin share and lab fees.
ideas.why_now: Polri and Kadin only passed 700-1,000+ kitchens in 2026; the mark-up ban, 4-hour rule and Kejagung case make unmanaged purchasing a career risk for generals and chairs; the moratorium on new kitchens means growth must come from running the existing ones better.
ideas.wedge: Kadin's kitchens in 3T and provincial clusters (business-led, less politically charged than Polri): a central lab and master supply agreement for 50 kitchens in one province, plus a lender dashboard for the Himbara bank behind them.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Per kitchen about $12k fee plus 2.5% of about $300k = $19.5k a year, so $100M needs about 5,100 kitchens. Institutional groups hold roughly 4,000-5,000 kitchens if targets are met, so this needs nearly all of them: 18% of all kitchens but only 4-6 signatures. As a principal supply contract, $100M of revenue is about 25% of the Polri-plus-Kadin ingredient flow (about $0.8B at 2,200 portions). Heroic and politically exposed.
ideas.who_does_it_today: In-house HQ logistics (Polri's food-security warehouses, farms and feed mills), BGN's SIPGN and Peruri-managed IoT, Telkom, IDSurvey (Sucofindo and Surveyor Indonesia offered QA support in April 2025), consulting firms. No private franchise-toolkit vendor found.
ideas.why_they_lose: In-house HQ units move at command speed, not lab speed, and attract ICW and KPK attention; BUMN IT sells software; Sucofindo-type inspectors audit but do not procure or train.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (embedded in an HQ's operating manual and loan covenants) plus scale economies in procurement; counter-positioning against in-house build (they would have to admit it failed).
ideas.earned_secret: The cap of 10 kitchens per yayasan, not the market, fragmented the operator base: the only enterprise accounts in this industry are institutions. Two signatures cover 8-10% of the programme; the Bessemer 'shooting star' playbook is to win a few huge accounts, then widen into the system of record. It has not happened because the groups only reached scale this year and believe they can build in-house.
ideas.first_90_days: Warm introduction through Kadin's MBG team; offer a 50-kitchen pilot (central lab plus lender dashboard) at cost; run a reputational screen before any Polri discussion; recruit a former police logistics officer and a former bank covenant manager. Check unverified premises: the Polri exemption from the 10-kitchen cap, conflict-of-interest rules for foundations led by officers' spouses, and whether service fees may sit in the at-cost line.

ideas.title: Java-to-3T protein corridor (own the logistics where infrastructure is weak)
ideas.one_liner: Own the chilled lane that ships Java's egg and chicken surplus to the frontier kitchens where BGN says the same programme costs up to three times as much.
ideas.customer: 3T kitchens in Papua, Maluku, NTT and Sulawesi: 480 activated from 2 Oct 2026 (211 independent mitra, 269 remote units) across 16 provinces; ministry sources cite 1,703 (another says 352) 3T kitchens in the pipeline and a presidential target of 2,500 kitchens in Papua was reported (unverified).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The kitchen's VA with an indexed budget (BGN is preparing an ingredient cost-of-living index and a rent incentive for remote areas), signed by the Kepala SPPG and mitra; at scale a master supply agreement with BGN's 3T programme office, a Danantara-financed kitchen programme, or Polri/TNI units building kitchens in Papua.
ideas.problem: Eligible local sellers barely exist in remote kecamatan, so the local-first rule falls through to 'outside province' with a trader taking a 2-3x mark-up; an LPG shortage halted NTT kitchens in May; poisonings in Jayapura and Depapre (Aug) cost kitchen heads their jobs; meanwhile Java has an egg and chicken surplus (Blitar farmers gave away 1M eggs) that the state is begging kitchens to absorb.
ideas.solution: Contract reefer slots on Pelni/Tol Laut from Surabaya and Makassar to cold-store hubs in Jayapura, Sorong, Ambon, Kupang and Merauke; feed them from Blitar egg cooperatives and East Java slaughterhouses; run last-mile trucks and boats on a published delivery calendar (menus and school holidays are public); sell frozen chicken, graded or pasteurised eggs and dry goods at the indexed price with batch traceability. Later add local fish and sago.
ideas.why_now: 3T activation on 2 Oct; moratorium elsewhere pushes growth east; 12 Aug poultry circular plus the egg surplus; the cost index and rent incentive are being set now; eastern kitchens cannot meet the 4-hour rule without reliable inputs.
ideas.wedge: One lane, Surabaya to Jayapura/Sorong, for 20 of the newly activated independent kitchens, frozen chicken and eggs only. First 10 customers: independent mitra in Papua and NTT plus Polri's Papua kitchens.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) 1,703 kitchens x 1,800 portions x 220 days x an indexed Rp20k per portion (about 2x Java) = $0.84B a year. $100M of revenue is 12% of that flow, at 15-20% gross margin for the logistics premium. If only 352 3T kitchens materialise the pool is about $0.17B and the idea fails; that count is the main uncertainty.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Makassar/Bugis and Surabaya trading networks, Pelni and Tol Laut (shipping only), Bulog (rice), Pertamina (LPG), Japfa and Charoen through distributors, provincial BUMD logistics, Polri's food-security warehouses, TNI/Agrinas. No cold-chain operator contracted to 3T kitchens found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Traders have no cold chain, paperwork or price index; shipping lines do not run door-to-door or quality control; Polri warehouses serve Polri; integrators sell at Java prices to distributors.
ideas.moat: Scale economies in lane utilisation (menu calendars make volume predictable) plus cornered resource (contracted reefer slots and Papua cold stores that cannot be copied quickly).
ideas.earned_secret: Where logistics is weak the platform that owns it wins (Mercado Libre). A 3T kitchen is a captive, price-indexed buyer with a published calendar (SE 12/2026), and Java's surplus makes the outbound cheap; the real cost is empty containers and cold-chain gaps, which a scheduled lane converts into a utilisation problem.
ideas.first_90_days: Secure reefer slots Surabaya-Jayapura on Tol Laut/Pelni; contract a Blitar egg cooperative and an East Java slaughterhouse; lease a cold store in Jayapura; obtain the draft cost index from BGN's 3T office; pilot 10 kitchens and compute landed cost against the trader price. Check the unverified premise that Article 5's local-first sequence allows out-of-province purchase when no local seller qualifies, and who is the eligible seller of record for goods from Java.

ideas.title: Kitchen workforce employer-of-record: the liability BGN cannot take
ideas.one_liner: Become the legal employer, payroll and BPJS provider for the roughly 1.3M kitchen 'volunteers' so the yayasan chair stops carrying employer liability and the at-cost wage claim becomes audit-proof.
ideas.customer: About 13,000 yayasan/mitra responsible for about 47 workers per kitchen across 27,820 kitchens.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The yayasan chair, from the Rp3k-per-portion operating line (BGN already lets wages and BPJS premiums be reimbursed at cost); the Kepala SPPG co-approves in the VA.
ideas.problem: Komnas HAM (15 Jun 2026) says kitchen staff are workers, not volunteers; Keputusan 401.1/2025 makes the yayasan responsible for BPJS, yet 278,614 workers in 5,322 kitchens were unprotected in April; pay is cash, below minimum wage in places, and a worker hurt commuting in Langkat was uncovered. At-cost wage claims are also an audit risk: ghost volunteers are the classic leak and the Attorney General is looking.
ideas.solution: An employer-of-record plus instant-pay rail: contract the workers, pay daily to bank or e-wallet, face-and-QR attendance matched to 02:00 starts, BPJS JKK/JKM (Rp16,800 a month), PPh 21, injury response, and an at-cost invoice pack (hours, pay slips, bank proofs) a Kepala SPPG and KPPN can accept. Optional earned-wage access and micro-insurance on top.
ideas.why_now: Komnas HAM statement; BPJS mandate; Kejagung case; 02:00 attendance rules; cooperation-agreement renewals this month.
ideas.wedge: Yayasan with 5-10 kitchens in one province, introduced by BSI/BNI relationship managers worried about their loans and by the mitra association.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Wage pool = 47 workers x Rp100k a day (assumed, derived from the Rp3k operating line; no official rate found) x 220 days x 27,820 kitchens = $1.8B. As an employer-of-record booking gross billings (like a staffing firm), $100M of revenue is 5.5% of the wage pool, about 1,530 kitchens. Net take is about 6% of payroll, so $100M of net revenue needs essentially 100% of the pool. Gross revenue is easy, profit is not.
ideas.who_does_it_today: BPJS Ketenagakerjaan (insurance only), alih-daya outsourcing firms, payroll software (Mekari Talenta, Kledo), earned-wage-access fintechs (not verified for this niche), yayasan cash payroll.
ideas.why_they_lose: Payroll software does not take employer liability; outsourcers do not know at-cost reimbursement, VAs or BGN reporting; BPJS covers accidents but does not run payroll.
ideas.moat: Process power (compliance know-how under changing BGN rules) plus switching costs (payroll history, BPJS records, attendance data usable for credit).
ideas.earned_secret: BGN's refusal to say 'employee' is a budget decision: paying 1.3M workers a monthly minimum wage (about Rp3M, assumed) would cost about Rp50T against roughly Rp29T now, i.e. about Rp21T more in a budget being trimmed. The ambiguity therefore persists until a court or labour inspector forces it, and the first yayasan sanctioned will buy cover overnight.
ideas.first_90_days: Build with a labour lawyer and a BPJS Ketenagakerjaan partner; pilot ten kitchens in one regency with daily pay through a Himbara bank VA; get a KPPN/Kepala SPPG to accept the audit pack; approach the mitra association. Check unverified premises: whether an EOR may employ workers BGN calls volunteers, whether the employer fee is reimbursable at cost, and alih-daya licensing limits for core-business workers.

ideas.title: Mitra resolution operator: the special servicer banks and BGN cannot be
ideas.one_liner: Take management contracts over stalled, suspended and non-compliant kitchens from their owners and their banks, fix them, get them reinstated and share the restored incentive (weakest of the eight, flagged).
ideas.customer: Passive mitra (facility owners) and the special-assets units of Himbara banks. Pool: about 13,000 stalled kitchens (Rp8.7T at risk, partner-association figure), about 4,500 suspended in May, 1,999 closed 7 Sep for not registering, 504-plus closed permanently.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The mitra owner (fee from the restored Rp6M-a-day incentive) with the bank's head of special assets co-signing a workout letter; BGN's regional coordinator accepts the resubmission.
ideas.problem: Bank collateral is a single-use building plus a permit that lapses when the kitchen is closed, so foreclosure recovers cents; Kontan expects bad loans to rise from September. BGN suspends on any poisoning report without a hearing (mitra association complaint), promised a settlement scheme on 27 Jul but has not defined it, and cannot run kitchens itself.
ideas.solution: A hotel-management-style contract: we run the non-BGN half of the kitchen (facility, volunteer workforce, compliance, utilities, supply) for a fee, fix SLHS/IPAL/gas/BPJS, and resubmit for reinstatement. Use BGN's new yayasan-switch route (2 Oct) to place kitchens under a clean foundation. Stack the plant, hub, workforce and utility ideas as paid modules.
ideas.why_now: SLHS closure wave; bank NPL fear; cooperation-agreement renewals; exposure of per-tray yayasan fees; the moratorium makes each existing permit scarce.
ideas.wedge: Ten suspended kitchens referred by two banks' special-assets teams, paid 15% of the restored incentive for 24 months.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Per kitchen: 15% of the $82.5k restored incentive = $12.4k, plus about $5k compliance/utility margin and $4k workforce fee = about $21k a year. $100M needs about 4,700 kitchens: 17% of all kitchens and maybe 30% of reinstatable distressed ones. Heroic, and the pool is one-off until BGN allows steady-state management contracts.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Bank special-assets units, the mitra association (lobbying only), crowdfunding platforms Danamart and Bizhare (Danamart says it will only monitor existing projects), BGN's pending settlement scheme, Danantara's asset-management MoU (new builds). No private resolution operator found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Banks cannot operate or foreclose a permit; BGN cannot restructure 27k private contracts or run kitchens; the association cannot provide services; passive owners lack expertise.
ideas.moat: Process power (a standard turnaround playbook) and, if bank-sanctioned, a cornered resource (referral flow).
ideas.earned_secret: A bank loan officer knows the collateral is the permit and the VA stream, not the building. Banks see VA inflows daily and know which kitchens will fail 60-90 days ahead, but have no operator to hand them to; BGN has just opened the door for mitra to change yayasan.
ideas.first_90_days: Meet special-assets heads at BSI, BNI and BTN; write a standard turnaround checklist from the SLHS/IPAL/4-hour requirements; take three owners on 24-month contracts; clear the route with BGN. Legal premise (unverified, risky): transfers of operation without a handover document are disputed (Yayasan Garuda Muda Dharmagati case), permanently closed kitchens receive no payment, and the 10-kitchen cap per yayasan blocks ownership roll-up so only management contracts are possible and BGN may refuse them.

ideas.title: Telur Koperasi: farmer-cooperative egg grading, pasteurising and glut-buffer plant
ideas.one_liner: Build the processing plant that turns the state's forced egg demand into a stable business: grade, sanitise and pasteurise local eggs for kitchens, and freeze or dry the glut for industry.
ideas.customer: Kitchens in egg-producing provinces (East Java, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi) plus bakery and noodle makers who now import egg powder or frozen liquid egg.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The kitchen VA for graded and pasteurised egg (HAP-based price plus a service premium) approved by Kepala SPPG and yayasan; industrial buyers for powder and frozen product; a farmer-cooperative chair signs as seller of record; Bapanas and Kementan are policy sponsors, not payers.
ideas.problem: Eggs are the mandated protein (at least three times a week) but the programme pauses on weekends and school holidays while hens do not; in May-June farm-gate fell below cost and Blitar farmers gave away a million eggs; the state answered with decrees (HAP Rp26,500/kg, circulars threatening suspension, SE 14/2026) that force kitchens to buy but create no storage, grading or Salmonella control, even though BGN's analysis found Salmonella on eggs.
ideas.solution: A cooperative-owned plant: washing, UV sanitising, grading and coding of shell eggs; pasteurised liquid egg for omelettes and scrambles (labour-saving, Salmonella-safe); frozen liquid and spray-dried powder to soak up troughs and supply industry; cracks and downgrades (3-5% of volume, assumed) become product instead of waste. Offtake contracts follow the BGN holiday calendar so farmers know the next six weeks.
ideas.why_now: Egg price collapse (May-June); HAP and circulars (June-August); about 13% surplus forecast for 2026 (unverified); SE 12/2026 publishes the pause calendar; kitchens ordered to serve eggs three times a week.
ideas.wedge: One Blitar-Kediri-Tulungagung plant (leased breaking line plus grading) supplying 10-20 local kitchens (the local-first rule favours them) and one bakery buyer.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) MBG eggs: 60.6M beneficiaries x 132 egg-days = 8.0B eggs = 480 kt, worth $0.79B at HAP. At about Rp34k per kg of liquid-egg equivalent, $100M is 47 kt of liquid egg = 0.89B eggs = 11% of MBG egg demand (0.7% of national output), i.e. two 100k-eggs-per-hour lines on two shifts; capex about $12-20M. Gross margin about 10-12% ($10-12M); the HAP floor limits the premium kitchens will pay (about +16% over shell egg), so adoption depends on safety and labour savings.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Intan Kenkomayo (Japfa joint venture; pasteurised liquid egg and mayonnaise), Japfa and Charoen's own egg operations, imports of frozen liquid egg (441 t in 2021) and egg powder (flagged by parliament in 2023), Pinsar and cooperative direct-sale deals in East Java, government decrees. No cooperative-owned processing at MBG scale found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Integrators compete with independent farmers and are not the micro/small/cooperative sellers SE 14/2026 favours; Intan Kenkomayo serves bakeries and horeca; farmers lack processing assets and credit.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against integrators (cooperative ownership qualifies for the mandate) plus cornered resource (offtake contracts and processing assets).
ideas.earned_secret: An egg trader knows the price signal is a WhatsApp rumour that moves farm-gate in hours, that cracks and downgrades are where the margin lives, and that the programme's pauses are scheduled, so the glut is predictable. Only someone who can store (frozen, dried) can profit from a predictable glut.
ideas.first_90_days: Form a cooperative-of-record with Blitar egg cooperatives; lease a used 30k-eggs-per-hour breaking line; sample 10 kitchens with graded and liquid egg and test kitchen-head acceptance. Check unverified premises: that processed egg from a cooperative plant satisfies SE 14/2026 and the HAP rule (which target farmers and cooperatives), halal and food-safety certification for processors, and BGN menu acceptance of liquid egg.

ideas.title: Dapur Utilitas: IPAL, gas and water as a per-portion service
ideas.one_liner: Finance, own and operate each kitchen's wastewater plant, bulk gas and water treatment, and bill it per portion inside the at-cost operating line (flagged: needs about 16% of its pool).
ideas.customer: Mitra/yayasan of full-size kitchens, especially those suspended for IPAL or lacking reliable gas supply.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The mitra, from the Rp3k operating line (power, water and gas are reimbursable at cost); the yayasan chair signs a 5-7 year service contract; infrastructure funds and Danantara/Himbara are the capital providers.
ideas.problem: IPAL is mandatory from 2026 and cost Rp18-70M in one region, with substandard units common; 1,780 kitchens were suspended in April for IPAL or SLHS; 3 kg LPG is banned and 50 kg cylinders must be pre-ordered, with NTT kitchens halted in May; mitra capital is exhausted and banks will not finance single-purpose assets.
ideas.solution: Bundle wastewater (IPAL, grease trap, sludge removal, quarterly effluent tests), water treatment, bulk CNG/LPG skids with telemetry and induction/steam retrofits into one per-portion fee (Rp400-600, assumed) with a savings share against current energy cost. Each kitchen gets compliance evidence that Dinkes and the Environment Ministry accept.
ideas.why_now: IPAL enforcement; the LPG ban reiterated 27 Jul; the SLHS closure wave; PGN's CNG pilot (46 kitchens, claimed 15-20% savings) proves the product.
ideas.wedge: Two districts with PGN CNG access: sign ten kitchens for IPAL-as-a-service with CNG supply and no capex for the mitra.
ideas.path_to_100m: (A) Gas about $10.3k per full-size kitchen (a Magelang CNG example, Rp12M a month for 2,179 portions, scaled to 3,000 portions and 10 operating months), power about $7k (assumed), IPAL/water/waste about $5k: about $22k a year, so a roughly $610M pool across 27,820 kitchens. $100M is about 4,500 kitchens, 16% of the pool, with capital of about $110-180M ($25-40k per kitchen). Heroic.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Pertamina Patra Niaga (Bright Gas 50 kg/12 kg), PGN/Pertagas (CNG, pipeline), PLN, local IPAL contractors, PDAM and depot water vendors, Aneka Gas and Samator, regional task forces pushing IPAL. No bundler found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each incumbent sells one commodity through a network monopoly and none finances on-site assets or carries compliance; mitra cannot capex.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (installed assets under 5-7 year contracts) plus scale economies in procurement and maintenance.
ideas.earned_secret: The cost of non-compliance (a Rp6M-a-day incentive) dwarfs the capex of compliance ($1-4k for an IPAL), so the binding constraint is cash and know-how, not willingness to pay. A cheap gas price is worthless if the cylinder does not arrive.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign PGN/Perta Samtan as CNG supplier; design a standard IPAL module; fund ten kitchens; measure savings; approach an infrastructure fund. Check unverified premises: that utilities and service fees are reimbursable at cost, that LPG distribution outside Pertamina channels is permitted, and Kementerian LH effluent standards (Kepmen LH 276/2025).

verdicts.title: Shop Ledger: cross-shop carrier-health network, paid in 24 hours

competitors_found.name: cbCharge / Corporate Billing (SouthState Bank)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Pays repair, parts and tire shops fast and assumes the fleet's credit risk; fleet gets one monthly statement. Preferred vendor for NAPA Truck Service, HDA Truck Pride, PTP, Jasper; powers Fleetio Maintenance Billing Account. Already sees invoices across its shop base.
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: In business since 1995, owned by SouthState Bank (public); site shows 1,973 locations

competitors_found.name: Fullbay Payments (RoadSync + Stripe)
competitors_found.what_they_do: Embedded fleet checks, fleet cards, card and ACH acceptance inside the shop management system; Fullbay also acquired Pitstop telematics in 2026
competitors_found.scale_or_funding: 3,400+ Fullbay shops; Mainsail $23M growth round; RoadSync $30M Series B (Tiger Global, 2021)

competitors_found.name: TruckerCloud
competitors_found.what_they_do: Single API over 100+ telematics providers marketed for underwriting, so ELD-based credit scoring is available to any lender

competitors_found.name: Progressive Smart Haul
competitors_found.what_they_do: Already makes ELD data a condition of commercial insurance for some small fleets, proving carriers will consent to data-for-credit trades

verdicts.substitutes: Fleet cards (WEX, EFS, Comdata, T-Chek) with weekly settlement, cash/card at pickup, shop factoring lines, shops simply requiring payment before release. Fullbay and Motive/Samsara could add credit on top of data they own.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: $3.3B financed at 3% = $99M is correct arithmetic but the sizing fails. Fullbay's 3,400+ shops billed a claimed $5.04B (about $1.5M each); if 25-50% of that is credit-terms invoices to small fleets, $3.3B needs roughly 4,400-8,900 shops, 1.3x-2.6x Fullbay's entire installed base. '6.6% of outsourced spend' is really 15-25%+ of the credit-terms small-fleet slice. Needs a balance sheet through a freight recession with small-carrier bankruptcies rising.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: (1) Fullbay and cbCharge stay passive while the network signs 2,000+ shops (low-moderate). (2) ELD plus cross-shop behavior beats cbCharge's existing ledger enough to price at 2% and hold losses under 1% (unproven; backtest not done). (3) Warehouse funding at under 8% in a freight recession (moderate). (4) Expansion into parts, tire and dealer trade credit triples the volume base (plausible but those sellers have credit departments). Even all four give about $70M, not $100M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: The Fullbay/Stripe survey figures (31%, 61%, 30%, 13%) could not be found in any source after several searches. State commercial-financing disclosure laws (California, New York) not verified by me. Premise that existing tools underwrite 'on applications' is unverified and cbCharge sees every invoice in its network.
verdicts.deciding_reason: cbCharge has done 24-hour pay with fleet credit risk since 1995 and already holds the cross-shop ledger; the ELD score is a feature incumbents can copy, and $100M exceeds Fullbay's whole installed base.

picks.from_title: The neutral LTSS manager for plans that compete with Elevance

picks.one_liner: A plan-owned-by-nobody HCBS manager with plan co-investors and a firewalled data model, replacing the independent CareBridge that Elevance bought.

Product: real-time visit and authorization data across every EVV aggregator (not one owner's), same-day missed-shift response, continuity-based agency steering, fraud triage and a risk-adjusted shared-savings contract with a floor. Capital and governance: two or three non-Elevance plans co-invest in exchange for volume commitments, the CareBridge 2022 template, with a written data firewall and a governance seat per plan so neutrality is a contract term, not a slogan. Start with a 5,000-member pilot in one state, but price and fund it as the first contract toward 70-90k at-risk members, not a boutique. Add network, fraud and payroll-signal modules on the same data to lift net revenue per member.
picks.payer_and_signer: The plan: SVP/VP of LTSS or Medicaid chief medical officer, paid from medical-cost management and care-management budgets, out of savings against the plan's own HCBS and hospital trend.
picks.path_to_100m: CareBridge-implied net economics are about $1,100-1,500 per member-year (about 5% of ~$30k managed spend; my inference from a ~1x-revenue exit). $100M needs about 70-90k at-risk members, 60-80% of CareBridge's 2023 base of ~115k, or roughly 4% of managed-LTSS HCBS members if there are 1.5-2M (unverified).
