picks.competitors_and_edge: CareBridge/Carelon (17 states plus DC, says it serves all customers), HHAeXchange payer tools (no risk-taking, 180+ MCOs claimed), plans' in-house LTSS teams and Optum. Edge: a contractually neutral owner with rival-plan co-investors, EVV-aggregator-agnostic data, and a D-SNP-aligned buyer focus so savings are capturable.
picks.why_now: Elevance closed the CareBridge purchase on 2024-12-10; Anthem, Optum, CVS and Centene had co-invested in 2022, so three of those four now face a competitor-owned vendor. H.R.1 cuts of ~$911B over 2025-34 press plan margins and make a lower hospital and nursing-home trend on the sickest HCBS cohort more valuable. Renewal windows for existing CareBridge contracts are opening in 2026-2028.
picks.moat: Switching costs once a plan's HCBS data and workflows run on the system, process power in missed-shift response, and a neutrality guarantee an owned competitor cannot copy. Cornered resource only if plan co-investors commit volume.
picks.biggest_open_risk: Whether rival plans will move volume to a neutral vendor rather than keep CareBridge, build in-house or lean on Optum; secondary risks are capturing savings that accrue to Medicare and raising capital for at-risk contracts.

picks.title: Fiscal-intermediary consolidator with a payroll-certainty SLA
picks.one_liner: Buy a small or mid FI for past performance, re-platform it so EVV hours become payroll, and bid state FMS rebids on guaranteed first-payroll performance.
picks.sharpened_pitch: Run statewide participant-directed payroll as a consolidator, not a bid-from-zero startup. Step one is to acquire a small or mid fiscal intermediary with live state contracts and a clean record, because after New York every state director now scores past performance and day-one payroll risk above price. Step two is to re-platform it so EVV-approved hours flow straight into payroll, onboarding (I-9, W-4, background and exclusion checks) is a tracked pipeline measured in days, and exceptions are auto-resolved or routed with deadlines. Step three is to compete in the rolling wave of state FMS rebids (Kentucky is open now with a stated 2026-11-06 deadline, Ohio and others on five-year cycles) and to be the credible second operator if New York reopens after the June 2026 DOJ suit against PPL. Drop the blanket 30% under pricing: NY already pays $68.50 per member per month while Louisiana-type states pay $100-117. Sell a service-level guarantee instead: zero missed first payroll, onboarding in days, and a funded payroll backstop if the state pays late. Add MCO-delegated FMS as a second channel and cross-sell working capital later.
picks.payer_and_signer: State Medicaid director or developmental-disabilities director through competitive procurement, from the FMS administrative line with federal match; MCOs for delegated FMS.
picks.path_to_100m: About 85k participants at ~$100 blended PMPM ($1,200 a year), or half of a NY-class contract (250k x $68.50 x 12 = ~$205M a year). FMS-vendor pool is ~0.7-1.0M people (~$0.8-1.2B a year, my estimate), so $100M is ~8-12% of the vendor pool. Reference: GT Independence serves 60k+ participants and just took H.I.G. growth capital, implying the #2 player is roughly $60-90M. Median ~$20M from one acquisition plus one or two mid-size wins.
picks.competitors_and_edge: PPL (DW Healthcare/Linden-owned, NY sole FI), GT Independence (H.I.G.-backed), Acumen, Palco, Tempus, with HHAX at the EVV layer. Edge: fresher EVV-to-payroll architecture, an SLA story states can defend after New York, and optionality on a NY rebid; no free substitute exists.
picks.why_now: New York collapsed ~600 FIs into one and then was sued by DOJ (filed 2026-06-16); PPL settled an aide underpayment class action for $162M. States are consolidating and rebidding (WV 2024, NY 2025, OH and KY 2025-26), the self-directing population grew 23% from 2019 to 2023, and H.R.1 cost pressure favors cheaper administration.
picks.moat: Multi-year state contracts with switching costs (thousands of enrolled workers), scale economies in fixed software cost, process power in exception handling, and state past-performance references.
picks.biggest_open_risk: Winning contracts as a new or newly acquired operator against PE-backed incumbents that can cut price, in procurements that weight past performance heavily; a possible bundle by HHAX CarePay is a second threat.
picks.cheapest_next_test: Get the Kentucky RFP text and map the state fiscal-agent tracker for contract expiry dates; call one former state FMS program manager and two small FI owners (including a displaced NY FI) about acquisition or teaming terms. Zero build cost.

result.pool_note: The money is state and plan administration budgets, not a fee skimmed from aide wages. Ideas assuming 3-5% of spend, a $30 hour, or "only we hold the data" failed on checking; HHAX already owns the visit and payroll data. Survivors have a named signer, a precedent contract or exit, and a fresh shock.

result.pool_note: Real shock, but waste-lipid money sits with integrated players and balance-sheet traders. Middleman ideas cap near $50-60M net because merchant spreads are 1-3c/lb, not 5c, and gross sales are not revenue. Legal and data premises failed twice (co-processing is D5-only, FD-CIC covers crops only). Verification and credit layers already exist.
